docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go 1.27.2+ (the embedded llm-d router requires it) — Download Go
  • Git — for cloning the repository

docs.title: Build from Source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/inference-sim/inference-sim.git
cd inference-sim
go build -o blis main.go

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
BLIS reads model architecture configs from a local catalog checkout and makes no HuggingFace requests, so running a simulation needs no token and no network access. Set HF_TOKEN only when downloading a new model's config.json by hand to add a catalog entry, e.g. for a gated model such as Llama-2:

export HF_TOKEN=your_token_here

Public models (e.g., Qwen3) work without a token. See HuggingFace access tokens to create a token.

Air-gapped / offline environments

Nothing to do — BLIS never reaches the network to run a simulation. Every model's config.json comes from your local catalog checkout, and a model with no catalog entry is refused rather than fetched.

To simulate a model that is not yet catalogued, obtain its config.json on a machine with internet access, then commit it at <catalog>/models/<model>/config.json — where <catalog> is whatever directory you point --catalog / BLIS_CATALOG at.

docs.title: Locate the Model Catalog
docs.text:
blis run and blis replay must be told where the model catalog is — there is no default and no search path, so a run with neither --catalog nor BLIS_CATALOG is refused naming both forms. Clone the authoritative blis-catalog repository at the pinned release tag (see Catalog compatibility below) and point BLIS at the clone root:

git clone --branch 0.3.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-catalog.git
export BLIS_CATALOG=$PWD/blis-catalog   # or pass --catalog on every command

docs.title: Catalog compatibility
docs.text:
blis-catalog versions independently of BLIS and keeps releasing, so the documented clone names an explicit tag rather than whatever main happens to be. This is the one place the compatible version is stated; every other page's clone command pins the same tag.

Compatible blis-catalog release: 0.3.0 — release notes.

Why pin at all: BLIS parses every catalog file strictly (KnownFields(true)), and strict parsing is one-way — an added or renamed key in a future catalog schema is a hard load error, not a silently ignored field. An unpinned clone therefore lets a catalog release turn a blis run that worked yesterday into a startup failure with no change to BLIS itself. Pinning also makes results attributable: two people running the documented commands months apart read the same catalog. (blis run --metrics-path records the catalog's git revision and whether it was dirty — see Results; a --depth 1 tag clone still carries the revision, so that provenance is unaffected.)

BLIS prices every run with blis-latency-kernel, which additionally reads a blis-registry clone for its fitted coefficients (--registry, required). Compatible blis-registry release: v0.2.0, the release blis-latency-kernel v0.3.0 (the version go.mod pins, with blis-schemas v0.5.0, whose deployment router: block configures the llm-d router) is tested against; that pair is recorded in the kernel's own testdata/upstream.lock, and this repository's test suite holds its vendored catalog and registry to it.

git clone --branch v0.2.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry.git

Upgrading to a newer catalog release is deliberately opt-in: clone the newer tag, run your workload against it, and if it works, bump the tag on the line above — the guard test then requires every documented clone command to match, so no page is left behind. Nothing stops you pointing --catalog at a main checkout or a scratch clone of your own; the pin is what the documentation promises, not a restriction the binary enforces.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Every blis run and blis replay names a scenario: a blis-schemas Scenario + Deployment YAML (two documents) that states the model, the cluster's hardware, fabric, nodes and GPUs per node, the coefficient sets that price it, the engine version, and each pool's role, parallelism and engine settings. --scenarios <dir> is any directory of scenario YAMLs and --scenario <file name> picks one in it. This repository ships ready-to-run scenarios in examplescenarios/ (speculative ones pin their acceptance, so no --speculative-* flag is needed): deepseek-v4.1-flash-h100-tp8-dspark5.yaml (the quickstart), an MoE gpt-oss-120b-h100-fp4-vllm-tp2.yaml, a deepseek-v4-pro-b300-fp4-vllm-tp4-mtp2.yaml, a P/D glm-5-h200-3p1d-ib.yaml, and a multi-node kimi-k3-h200-tp8dp4ep32-balanced.yaml. See examplescenarios/README.md for details.

docs.title: Verify the Build
docs.text:
./blis run --scenarios examplescenarios \
  --scenario deepseek-v4.1-flash-h100-tp8-dspark5.yaml \
  --registry $PWD/blis-registry --catalog $PWD/blis-catalog \
  --num-requests 10

blis carries the repository's defaults.yaml (the LoRA cost constants) compiled in, so it runs from any directory. A defaults.yaml in the working directory, or --defaults-filepath <file>, takes precedence over the compiled-in copy.

You should see JSON output on stdout containing fields like ttft_mean_ms, e2e_mean_ms, and responses_per_sec. This confirms BLIS is working correctly.

mkdocs serve

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Run your first BLIS simulation in 30 seconds.

No credentials or network access are needed to run a simulation: BLIS reads each model's architecture from a local checkout of the model catalog and makes no HuggingFace requests. (HF_TOKEN matters only if you are downloading a new — possibly gated — model's config.json by hand to add a catalog entry.)

docs.title: Set up the catalog, registry and scenarios
docs.text:
Every blis run / blis replay needs three things besides the binary:

  • the catalog — a clone of blis-catalog (models, chips, fabrics, storage devices, workload presets), located by --catalog <path> or BLIS_CATALOG (the flag wins; there is no default and no search path);
  • the registry — a clone of blis-registry (the fitted coefficients), passed as --registry;
  • a scenario — a blis-schemas Scenario + Deployment YAML naming the model, hardware, parallelism and engine settings, picked with --scenario <file name> from --scenarios <dir>.
git clone --branch 0.3.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-catalog.git
git clone --branch v0.2.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry.git
export BLIS_CATALOG=$PWD/blis-catalog   # or pass --catalog on every command
export SCENARIOS=examplescenarios

A scenario directory can be any directory of scenario YAMLs. $SCENARIOS above is this repository's ready-to-run set (examplescenarios/). The clones pin the releases BLIS is tested against — see Catalog compatibility.

docs.title: Single-Instance Simulation
docs.text:
./blis run --scenarios $SCENARIOS \
  --scenario deepseek-v4.1-flash-h100-tp8-dspark5.yaml --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 10 --num-requests 100

This runs 100 requests at 10 requests/second through one DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash engine on an 8-GPU H100 node (FP8, vLLM, TP8 with expert parallelism and DSpark speculative decoding), priced by blis-latency-kernel.

The scenario states the deployment

There are no --model, --hardware or --tp flags. Model, hardware, parallelism, block size, batch limits, max model length, prefix caching, cache dtype and speculative decoding all come from the scenario; the KV block budget comes from the kernel. A model runs only if it is in the catalog — nothing is fetched at run time.

docs.title: Reading the Output
docs.text:
BLIS prints diagnostic logs to stderr and results to stdout. You'll see log lines (prefixed with INFO or WARN) followed by a === Simulation Metrics === header and pretty-printed JSON:

Latency metrics (all in milliseconds, reported as mean/p90/p95/p99):

Field What It Measures ttft_mean_ms, ttft_p99_ms Time to First Token — how long until the first output token is generated. Lower is better for interactive use. e2e_mean_ms, e2e_p99_ms End-to-End latency — total time from request arrival to final output token. itl_mean_ms, itl_p99_ms Inter-Token Latency — time between consecutive output tokens. Lower means smoother streaming. scheduling_delay_p99_ms Wait time from request arrival until processing begins (includes any queueing).

Throughput:

Field What It Measures responses_per_sec Completed requests per second. tokens_per_sec Output tokens generated per second. completed_requests How many requests finished within the simulation window. total_input_tokens, total_output_tokens Total tokens processed across all completed requests.

Health indicators:

Field What It Measures preemption_count Number of times a running request was evicted to make room for others. Non-zero suggests the system is overloaded. dropped_unservable Requests rejected because they were too large for the configured memory or context length. still_queued, still_running Requests not yet completed when the simulation ended. Non-zero means the workload outlasted the simulation window.

docs.title: Cluster Mode
docs.text:
Scale to 4 instances behind the router. --num-instances cannot exceed the scenario pool's rank capacity (pool nodes × gpus_per_node / (pp × tp × pcp)); the single-node scenario above is one rank, so this uses the two-node gpt-oss-120b-h100-fp4-vllm-tp2-2node.yaml (2 × 8 ÷ TP2 = 8 ranks, up to eight instances):

./blis run \
  --scenarios examplescenarios \
  --scenario gpt-oss-120b-h100-fp4-vllm-tp2-2node.yaml --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 \
  --rate 100 --num-requests 500

This simulates a 4-instance cluster receiving 100 requests/second. Every cluster run routes with the llm-d router (the Endpoint Picker) embedded in the simulator; with no router configuration it uses the router's built-in default configuration (queue, KV-cache utilization and prefix-cache scorers). A real deployment's router configuration is stated by the scenario's router: block and pool labels; see Routing.

Multi-instance output format

In cluster mode, BLIS prints one JSON block per instance plus a cluster-level summary (5 blocks total for 4 instances). The cluster summary has "instance_id": "cluster". If piping to jq, use --slurp to handle multiple JSON objects: ./blis run ... 2>/dev/null | jq --slurp '.[] | select(.instance_id == "cluster")' to extract the cluster summary.

docs.title: Try Different Configurations
docs.text:
# Higher traffic rate
./blis run --scenarios examplescenarios \
  --scenario gpt-oss-120b-h100-fp4-vllm-tp2-2node.yaml --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 8 --rate 500 --num-requests 2000

# With decision tracing (see where each request was routed)
./blis run --scenarios examplescenarios \
  --scenario gpt-oss-120b-h100-fp4-vllm-tp2-2node.yaml --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 100 --num-requests 500 \
  --trace-level decisions --summarize-trace

# A different deployment: pick another scenario (single-node TP2: up to 4 instances)
./blis run --scenarios examplescenarios \
  --scenario gpt-oss-120b-h100-fp4-vllm-tp2.yaml --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 2 --rate 100 --num-requests 500

docs.title: Tutorial: Capacity Planning
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through a complete capacity planning exercise: determining how many inference instances you need to serve a target request rate while meeting latency SLOs.

Scenario: You're deploying Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on H200 GPUs (FP8, vLLM, TP4). Your SLO is TTFT p99 < 500ms. You need to find the minimum number of instances for 40 requests/second.

Set up the catalog and registry first

Every command below needs the catalog (--catalog or BLIS_CATALOG) and the registry (--registry). Clone both at their pinned releases — git clone --branch 0.3.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-catalog.git and git clone --branch v0.2.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry.git — and run export BLIS_CATALOG=$PWD/blis-catalog once. See Quick Start and Catalog compatibility.

docs.title: Step 0: A Scenario Big Enough for a Cluster
docs.text:
The scenario states how many nodes the deployment has, and --num-instances cannot exceed the pool's rank capacity (pool nodes × gpus_per_node / (pp × tp × pcp)). The kernel's single-node llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml allows only two instances, so this tutorial uses the committed fixture testdata/scenarios/llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml: the same model, engine settings and TP4 on four 8-GPU H200 nodes over 400G InfiniBand — up to eight instances.

For other shapes, copy any scenario into a directory of your own, raise cluster.nodes and the pool's nodes, and add a cluster.fabric (a multi-node cluster must name one, e.g. ib-400g); --scenarios accepts any directory of scenario YAMLs.

docs.title: Step 1: Estimate Instance Capacity
docs.text:
Before scaling up, measure the throughput of a single instance under load. Run enough requests at a high arrival rate to saturate the instance — this reveals the maximum throughput with continuous batching:

./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 500 --num-requests 2000

Check the responses_per_sec value in the output. For this deployment with the default workload (512 input / 512 output tokens), a saturated instance handles roughly 11 requests/second.

Why measure at high load?

With continuous batching, throughput depends on batch size. At low arrival rates (e.g., --rate 2), requests trickle in one at a time and the instance processes only ~2 req/s — not because it's slow, but because there's nothing else to batch. At saturation, many concurrent requests share each decode step, amortizing overhead. Always measure capacity under load.

This means for 40 req/s, you need at minimum ceil(40/11) = 4 instances. Let's verify with simulation.

--rate is the total arrival rate

The --rate flag specifies the total arrival rate across the cluster, not per-instance. With --rate 40 --num-instances 4, each instance receives roughly 40/4 = 10 req/s (distributed by the llm-d router).

docs.title: Step 2: Baseline — Single Instance at Low Load
docs.text:
./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 2 --num-requests 50

At 2 req/s (well below capacity), TTFT p99 is around 120ms and mean ITL around 14ms. Note these values — this is your best-case baseline that won't improve further with more instances.

docs.title: Step 3: Scale Up and Find the Saturation Point
docs.text:
Run simulations at increasing instance counts for 40 req/s:

# 2 instances (20 req/s per instance vs ~11 saturated capacity → overloaded)
./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 2 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000

# 4 instances (10 req/s per instance → just under capacity)
./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000

# 8 instances (5 req/s per instance → comfortable headroom)
./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 8 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000

Compare the cluster-level ttft_p99_ms and itl_mean_ms across runs:

  • 2 instances: TTFT p99 around 60 seconds — the per-instance arrival rate (20 req/s) far exceeds capacity (~11 req/s), so requests queue up and wait
  • 4 instances: TTFT p99 around 130ms — the queue no longer grows, but each instance runs large batches, so mean ITL (~28ms) is double the baseline
  • 8 instances: TTFT p99 around 120ms and mean ITL around 17ms — close to baseline

Understanding saturation

Saturation means requests arrive faster than they can be served, so the queue grows continuously. In queueing theory terms, the per-instance excess rate is excess = λ/k - μ, where λ is the total arrival rate (40 req/s), k is the instance count, and μ is the per-instance service rate (~11 req/s). When excess > 0, the queue grows at that rate and TTFT degrades.

The improvement from 2→4 instances is dramatic (60s → 130ms) because the excess rate goes from ~9 req/s per instance to below zero. Past that point, more instances buy smaller batches — lower ITL — rather than lower TTFT.

docs.title: Step 4: Identify the Bottleneck Type
docs.text:
When TTFT is high, there are three possible causes:

  1. Queue saturation — arrival rate exceeds service capacity → add instances
  2. Memory saturation — KV cache preemptions degrade throughput → add KV blocks or reduce batch size
  3. Compute saturation — step time dominates → reduce batch size or use chunked prefill

Check the output for clues:

  • High preemption_count → memory saturation
  • High scheduling_delay_p99_ms → queue saturation (requests waiting in the WaitQ)
  • Low preemption_count + low scheduling_delay + high TTFT → compute saturation

docs.title: Step 5: Compare Router Configurations
docs.text:
Every cluster run routes with the llm-d router; its configuration is an EndpointPickerConfig named by the scenario's router: block (see Routing); the scenarios in examples/llm-d/scenarios/ name the configurations in examples/llm-d/. With 4 instances at 40 req/s (near saturation), compare the router's built-in default configuration (queue, KV-cache utilization and prefix-cache scorers) with a load-only configuration:

# The router's built-in default configuration
./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000

# Load-only: queue-scorer and kv-cache-utilization-scorer
./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node-load-only.yaml \
  --scenarios examples/llm-d/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000

With uniform workloads (same prompt/output distribution), router configurations produce similar results because all instances are roughly equally loaded. Routing differentiation becomes meaningful with heterogeneous workloads. Prefix-cache scoring pulls same-prefix requests onto the instance that already caches the prefix — which helps when there are many prefix groups, and can hurt when there is only one:

./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node-prefix-affinity.yaml \
  --scenarios examples/llm-d/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000 \
  --prefix-tokens 512

Here every request shares the same 512-token prefix. When the prefix-cache weight dominates the load-balancing weights, requests concentrate on the instance holding the prefix. Compare ttft_p99_ms against the load-only configuration with the same --prefix-tokens 512, and watch for this hot-spotting whenever prefix weights dominate load weights.

docs.title: Step 6: Evaluate with Fitness Scores
docs.text:
For automated comparison across many configurations, use fitness evaluation:

./blis run \
  --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 8 --rate 40 --num-requests 4000 \
  --fitness-weights "p99_ttft:3,mean_e2e:1,throughput:2"

The fitness score is a weighted sum of normalized metrics — higher is better. Each latency metric is normalized to a [0, 1] range using 1/(1+x/1000), and throughput is normalized to [0, 1] using throughput/max_throughput. With weights p99_ttft:3, mean_e2e:1, throughput:2, the score is a weighted sum out of a theoretical maximum of 6.0 (the sum of all weights).

Fitness score normalization

The 1/(1+x/1000) normalization compresses large raw differences into small score differences. A 38% TTFT improvement may appear as only an 8% fitness score difference. Always examine raw metrics (ttft_p99_ms, e2e_mean_ms, responses_per_sec) alongside fitness scores when making capacity decisions.

docs.title: Step 7: Validate Against Your SLO
docs.text:
Your SLO: TTFT p99 < 500ms at 40 req/s.

From the simulations above, 4 instances already meet the SLO (TTFT p99 ~130ms), and 8 instances also bring ITL back near baseline. Add 20-30% headroom for traffic spikes (real deployments see bursty traffic that exceeds the Poisson assumption).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Measure capacity under load — run at high arrival rates (e.g., --rate 500) to measure saturated throughput; low-load measurements underestimate capacity due to small batch sizes
  2. Saturation is non-linear — TTFT degrades super-linearly as you approach capacity. Scaling from 2→4 instances can cut TTFT p99 by more than 400x, not just 2x, because the per-instance excess rate drops below zero
  3. Check the bottleneck type — preemption count, scheduling delay, and raw TTFT tell you whether to add instances, add memory, or tune batch size
  4. Routing matters for heterogeneous workloads — with uniform traffic, router configurations produce similar results; with prefix-heavy or mixed-SLO workloads, prefix-aware and load-aware configurations differ sharply — in either direction
  5. Deterministic replay — use --seed to get identical results for A/B comparisons

docs.title: Admission Control
docs.text:
Admission and flow control in a cluster simulation are the llm-d router's. BLIS runs the router's own admission controller and flow-control layer (see Routing); it has no admission logic of its own. This page covers how the router admits, queues and sheds simulated requests, how BLIS SLO classes reach it, and how its outcomes are counted. Single-instance runs have no router and admit every request.

The mapping from each removed BLIS admission and flow-control flag to its llm-d configuration is the table in Routing: From BLIS's former routing features.

docs.title: Request priority: SLO classes and InferenceObjectives
docs.text:
Each request carries an SLO class (slo_class on its workload client). The router receives it as the x-llm-d-inference-objective header and the request's tenant as x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id. The router turns the objective name into a priority by looking up the InferenceObjective of that name; a request whose objective it does not know gets priority 0. A priority below 0 makes a request sheddable.

The router reconciles InferenceObjective objects only for an InferencePool, so priorities apply when the EPP flags (router.epp_flags) select a pool with --pool-name and the manifests (router.manifests) carry the pool and its objectives. With the default standalone pool (--endpoint-selector), every request has priority 0 and nothing is sheddable. examples/llm-d/inferencepool.yaml holds a pool over every simulated pod and one objective per BLIS SLO class, at the same priorities as BLIS's engine SLO priority map. A scenario selects it with --pool-name=blis-pool --pool-namespace=default in router.epp_flags and names it in router.manifests, as examples/llm-d/scenarios/llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node-inferencepool.yaml does:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node-inferencepool.yaml \
  --scenarios examples/llm-d/scenarios \
  --registry $PWD/blis-registry --num-instances 2 --workload-spec my-workload.yaml
SLO class Objective priority Sheddable critical 4 No standard 3 No batch -1 Yes sheddable -2 Yes background -3 Yes

The router reconciles both served InferenceObjective versions, llm-d.ai/v1 (spec.poolRefs) and llm-d.ai/v1alpha2 (spec.poolRef), with their CRD defaults applied (see Routing).

docs.title: Legacy admission (flow control off)
docs.text:
With the flowControl feature gate off (the default), the router's legacy admission controller checks each request before scheduling: a sheddable request is rejected when the saturation detector reports the pool saturated (saturation >= 1). Non-sheddable requests are never rejected by it. The saturation detector is utilization-detector unless the configuration names another (concurrency-detector, max-saturation-detector); the utilization detector's thresholds are its queueDepthThreshold (default 5 waiting requests) and kvCacheUtilThreshold (default 0.8) parameters. It reads the metrics the router scrapes from the simulated engines, so its view is as old as the last scrape (--refresh-metrics-interval).

An admitter plugin (probabilistic-admitter) can reject requests in addition.

docs.title: Flow control
docs.text:
With featureGates: [flowControl] in the EndpointPickerConfig, the router queues requests instead of shedding them. Requests are grouped into priority bands (one per objective priority, from the reconciled InferenceObjectives) and, within a band, into flows by fairness ID. A request is dispatched when the saturation detector reports capacity; otherwise it waits. The flowControl block configures:

Setting What it does maxRequests, maxBytes Global capacity. A request arriving at a full queue is rejected. priorityBands[] (priority, maxRequests, maxBytes, defaultRequestTTL, fairnessPolicyRef, orderingPolicyRef) Per-band capacity, queue-wait budget and policies. defaultPriorityBand and defaultNegativePriorityBand set the bands not listed. defaultRequestTTL Queue-wait budget (default 60s). A request that cannot dispatch within it is shed. 0s disables it. saturationDetector.pluginRef The detector that gates dispatch. usageLimitPolicyPluginRef static-usage-limit-policy, soft-reflective-ceiling-policy bandSelectionPolicyPluginRef strict-band-selection-policy, priority-holdback-policy

Fairness policies are global-strict-fairness-policy and round-robin-fairness-policy; ordering policies are fcfs-ordering-policy, edf-ordering-policy and slo-deadline-ordering-policy. The dispatch tick (1 ms) and the expiry sweep (1 s) are the router's own. With in-flight eviction (enableEviction), when higher-priority requests are blocked by saturation the router revokes in-flight sheddable (priority < 0) requests: BLIS observes the router's eviction signal, aborts the request on its engine in a fresh event (its KV blocks and adapter pin are released), ends the router's response with the eviction cause, and counts it as Gateway Evicted (in-flight) (INV-1). A victim not on an engine at that instant is retried at the router's next step; one that completes first is not revoked.

apiVersion: llm-d.ai/v1
kind: EndpointPickerConfig
featureGates:
- flowControl
flowControl:
  maxRequests: "200"
  defaultRequestTTL: 10s
  defaultPriorityBand:
    fairnessPolicyRef: round-robin-fairness-policy
plugins:
- type: round-robin-fairness-policy
- type: queue-scorer
- type: max-score-picker
schedulingProfiles:
- name: default
  plugins:
  - pluginRef: queue-scorer
  - pluginRef: max-score-picker

docs.title: Outcomes and INV-1
docs.text:
Every request the router does not dispatch lands in one bucket of request conservation (INV-1):

Router outcome Bucket Anomaly counter Legacy admission shed a sheddable request, or an admitter rejected it rejected_requests Rejected Requests (Admission) No endpoint can serve it routing_rejections Rejected Requests (Routing) Flow control rejected it: queues at capacity gateway_queue_rejected Gateway Queue Rejected It waited in flow control past its TTL gateway_expired Gateway Expired (TTL) It is still queued in flow control at the end of the run gateway_queue_depth --

Admission rejections and TTL expiries are also counted per SLO class (Shed (<class>)). See Results for the output format.

docs.title: Engine-level priority
docs.text:
Separately from the router, each instance's scheduler uses an engine priority derived from the SLO class through SLOPriorityMap: critical 4, standard 3 (also for an empty or unknown class), batch -1, sheddable -2, background -3. Priority scheduling and priority preemption use it (see Scheduling & Priority). Override classes in the policy bundle (--policy-config), in the range -100 to 100; unlisted classes keep their defaults:

priority:
  slo_priorities:
    batch: 0       # raise batch above the other negative classes
    critical: 10

priority.slo_priorities affects only the engines. The router's priorities come from the InferenceObjectives, so to change both, change both.

docs.text:

  • Cluster Simulation -- the pipeline around the router
  • Results -- anomaly counters and per-SLO output

docs.title: Archon PR Review
docs.text: Archon is an architecture analysis tool that extracts package-level dependency graphs from Go repositories and diffs them between commits. The /archon-pr-review CI command runs Archon on a pull request and reports whether the PR changes the architecture or is purely internal.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Comment on any PR:

/archon-pr-review

The GitHub Action runs automatically and posts the results as a PR comment. Re-running /archon-pr-review updates that same comment in place rather than adding a new one, so a long-running PR keeps one current report instead of a stack of near-identical ones.

The command must begin a line to count as an invocation — on its own line, either first in the comment or after a report it follows. Arguments still work on that line (/archon-pr-review --archon-ref <ref>).

Mentioning the command inside a sentence, a table or a quoted review does not trigger a run, so you can discuss it in a PR thread without re-reviewing the PR (#1675). One case is not covered: a line that begins with the command and then carries on in prose — a report opening /archon-pr-review issued NO_CHANGE … — still fires. The gate is a workflow expression, and expressions have no regex, so "alone on its line" cannot be expressed. When quoting a report whose line starts with the command, prefix the line (>) or indent it; either is enough to stop it being read as a directive. That last case is deliberate rather than overlooked — a line-leading occurrence is a directive under the rule above — and the stricter reading, where the command must be alone on its line, is tracked in #1810.

Not yet in force

The anchoring described above is carried as a pending patch, .github/archon-trigger-anchor.patch, because the delivery runner's token cannot write to .github/workflows/. Until a maintainer applies it, the live gate still matches the command anywhere in a comment body, so prose mentions do trigger runs. Applying it is tracked in #1809; remove this note in the same commit that applies the patch.

Each round's full body is also written to its own workflow run's job summary. That is retention-bound, not an archive: it disappears when the run is aged out under the repository's retention policy. If you need a round preserved, quote it in a PR comment.

docs.title: Empty Delta (No Architectural Change)
docs.text:
If the PR only changes internal implementation (file renames, function body rewrites, new files within existing packages without new exports), Archon reports:

No architectural change detected. Internal-only PR — fast-track eligible.

If tests (invariants) were added, removed, or modified, those are listed separately — even when the structure is unchanged.

docs.title: Non-Empty Delta (Architecture Changed)
docs.text:
If the PR changes package boundaries, Archon reports three sections:

1. Architectural Delta — What structurally changed:

  • + arrow A -> B [import] — new dependency between packages
  • - arrow A -> B [import] — removed dependency
  • + surface pkg.Func — package surface widened (new export)
  • - surface pkg.Func — package surface narrowed (export removed)
  • + box pkg / - box pkg — new or removed package

2. Blast Radius — For each changed package, how many other packages depend on it (directly and transitively). High blast radius means a change there affects many things.

3. Contract Evidence — For each interface (contract) in the codebase, which implementations are covered by a contract test and which are not. Gaps are flagged.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Determines the merge-base and PR head SHA
  2. Runs archon-go delta --json to detect structural changes
  3. If empty: posts fast-track message
  4. If non-empty: runs archon-go delta (human report), archon-go impact (blast radius per changed package), and archon-go evidence (contract test coverage)
  5. Posts combined output as a PR comment, editing the existing archon comment if one exists

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text:
• Witness-only changes are invisible. A file rename or function body edit within a package does not appear in the delta. Only boundary-crossing changes (new dependencies, new/removed exports, new/removed packages) are reported.
  • Deterministic. Same commits always produce the same output.
  • No LLM involved. Pure static analysis. For LLM-interpreted results, see /archon-pr-review-claude (#1540).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• The repository must be a Go module
  • The commenter must have write access to the repository
  • Archon is built from archon v0.1.0 during the CI run

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Issue: #1541
  • Future: #1540 — /archon-pr-review-claude feeds Archon output to Claude for a reasoned architectural review

docs.title: Cluster Simulation
docs.text:
This guide covers running multi-instance BLIS simulations — the full pipeline from request arrival through the llm-d router, per-instance scheduling, and metrics aggregation. Admission, routing and flow control are made by the llm-d router embedded in the simulator; see Routing with the llm-d Router.

# Quick example: 4-instance cluster with tracing
./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 100 --num-requests 500 \
  --trace-level decisions --summarize-trace

docs.title: Single-Instance vs Cluster Mode
docs.text: Setting Behavior --num-instances 1 (default) One instance behind the llm-d router: the router can only pick that instance, but its admission and flow control apply. With the default configuration it admits every request at once, and results equal a run without a router --num-instances N (N > 1) Every request passes through the llm-d router, which admits, queues (flow control) and routes it to an instance

docs.title: The Pipeline
docs.text:
Arrival → gateway latency → llm-d router → dispatch → Instance WaitQueue → Batch Formation → Step → Completion
                                 ↓                                              ↓
                              rejection                          KV Allocation + Latency Estimation
  1. A request arrives at the cluster.
  2. After --gateway-latency microseconds (default 0) the llm-d router sees it, as the Endpoint Picker would see a request Envoy hands it.
  3. The router runs its admission, flow control (when the flowControl feature gate is on) and scheduling profiles, and either picks an endpoint or rejects the request. A rejection lands in exactly one INV-1 bucket; see Admission Control.
  4. The picked instance enqueues the request; its own scheduler and batch formation take over.
Stage Controls Configured by Admission, flow control, routing Whether the request is admitted, how long it waits, which instance receives it The llm-d router's inputs: the scenario's router: block and pools[].labels; see the router's inputs Scheduling What order within the instance --scheduler, the policy bundle's priority section Batch Formation Which requests form the next batch scenario max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens

With no router inputs, the router uses its built-in default configuration over every simulated pod.

docs.title: Deployment Shape: Parallelism, DP and P/D
docs.text:
Each instance's shape comes from the scenario, not from flags: the pool's parallel block (tp, pp, dp, enable_expert_parallel) and its engine settings. blis-latency-kernel prices the step time and sizes the KV budget for that shape. --num-instances sets how many instances run; all instances of a pool are identical.

--num-instances must not exceed the scenario's rank capacity: pool nodes × gpus_per_node / (pp × tp × pcp). The single-node TP4 Llama scenario fits 2 instances; testdata/scenarios/llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml (4 H200 nodes over 400G InfiniBand, TP4) fits 8. For another shape, copy a scenario, raise cluster.nodes and the pool's nodes, and add a cluster.fabric.

Data parallelism (MoE only). A pool with dp > 1 becomes one replica per data-parallel rank, each sized as one vLLM EngineCore (its own KV budget and batch limits). dp > 1 on a dense model is refused.

Prefill/decode disaggregation. A scenario with prefill and decode pools runs one kernel per pool. Choose the topology with --prefill-instances and --decode-instances (whose sum must not exceed --num-instances); each must not exceed its pool's rank capacity, nodes × gpus_per_node / (pp × tp × pcp). The KV handoff is priced by the kernel's PDTransferTime over the scenario's fabric between the two instances' placements.

Which requests are disaggregated is the router's decision: give it an EndpointPickerConfig with the disagg-profile-handler, a P/D decider (always-disagg-pd-decider or prefix-based-pd-decider) and prefill and decode scheduling profiles. BLIS labels prefill and decode pods with llm-d.ai/role, so the prefill-filter and decode-filter plugins select them. examples/llm-d/pd.yaml disaggregates every request. This repository's testdata/scenarios/glm-5-h200-3p1d-ib.yaml is a 3P1D example whose router: block names such a configuration:

./blis run --scenario glm-5-h200-3p1d-ib.yaml --scenarios testdata/scenarios \
  --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --prefill-instances 3 --decode-instances 1 \
  --rate 10 --num-requests 100

Refused: a P/D topology over a colocated scenario; a disaggregated scenario without --prefill-instances/--decode-instances; prefill and decode pools that differ in block size, dp or draft configuration; shared (--prefill-decode-instances) or encode instances. KV offload works with P/D: each pool sizes the same tiers by its own bytes per block and prices them with its own kernel. The handoff follows NIXL: the decode side pulls only what its prefix cache lacks, the prefill side holds its KV until the pull completes, and with --pd-transfer-contention concurrent handoffs share the NIC and NVLink links they cross, which matters when a shared link (e.g. the decode node's NIC in xP1D) runs close to saturation. See Latency models.

docs.title: Node pools and multi-node placement
docs.text:
When node pools are configured (--policy-config with node_pools), every pool's gpu_type must equal the scenario's cluster.hardware, and gpu_type must be unique across pools.

An instance whose TP group exceeds a pool's gpus_per_node can occupy whole nodes across the same pool. This happens only as a fallback (BLIS first tries a single node in any matching pool) and only when tp is a whole multiple of gpus_per_node (e.g. tp=16 on 8-GPU nodes → 2 nodes), so every node carries an equal rank count — the shape vLLM's multiprocessing executor enforces. If tp ≤ gpus_per_node but the pool is merely fragmented, the instance is not spanned; it stays pending. A spanning instance is billed for every node it occupies (cost_per_hour × nodes_spanned). Node pools are blis run only: blis replay rejects node_pools.

docs.title: Scaling and Saturation
docs.text:
Instance scaling produces super-linear TTFT improvement near saturation, because the per-instance queue growth rate excess = λ/k - μ drops faster than linearly. For example, with a per-instance saturation rate μ = 17 req/s at λ = 200 req/s:

4 instances:  excess = 200/4 - 17  = 33 req/s per instance   → rapid queue growth
8 instances:  excess = 200/8 - 17  = 8 req/s per instance    → near saturation
12 instances: excess = 200/12 - 17 = -0.3 req/s per instance → balanced (sub-saturation)

At sub-saturation (excess ≤ 0): TTFT converges to its unloaded baseline and further scaling provides diminishing returns. Measure μ for your own scenario and workload.

docs.title: Admission Control
docs.text: Admission and flow control are the llm-d router's; see Admission Control.

docs.title: Gateway Latency
docs.text: --gateway-latency (µs, default 0) models the network and proxy hops between a request's arrival and the router's first look at it. The router itself takes zero simulated time to decide. --epp-scrape-jitter (µs, default 0) bounds a seeded phase offset of each endpoint's metrics collection.

docs.title: Decision Tracing
docs.text:
Log every routing decision, with the scores the router's primary scheduling profile gave every endpoint:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml \
  --scenarios testdata/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 100 --num-requests 500 \
  --trace-level decisions --summarize-trace --counterfactual-k 3

The trace summary shows: - Target Distribution — how many requests went to each instance - Mean/Max Regret — the best alternative endpoint's score minus the chosen endpoint's score

--counterfactual-k ranks the top-k endpoints by those scores.

Regret under the max-score picker

With max-score-picker the chosen endpoint is always the highest-scoring one, so regret is zero. Regret is non-zero only with pickers that may choose a lower-scoring endpoint (random-picker, weighted-random-picker).

docs.title: Event Ordering
docs.text:
The cluster uses (timestamp, priority, seqID) ordering for deterministic event processing:

  • Cluster events at time T process before instance events at time T
  • Same-time instance ties broken by lowest instance index
  • This ensures determinism (INV-6) but means results differ from a simple M/M/k queueing model

docs.title: Work-Conserving Property
docs.text: BLIS is work-conserving (INV-8): it never idles while requests wait. After every step completion, if the WaitQ has requests, a new StepEvent is immediately scheduled. Real systems may have scheduling delays not modeled here.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Cluster Architecture — internal mechanics of the shared-clock event loop
  • Routing with the llm-d Router — the router's inputs, supported plugins and the signals it sees
  • Metrics & Results — understanding trace summaries and per-SLO metrics

docs.title: KV Cache & Memory Management
docs.text:
This guide covers KV cache allocation, prefix caching, tiered GPU+CPU offload, and chunked prefill — the memory subsystem that determines how many requests can run concurrently.

The examples use the canonical scenario from Getting Started; any scenario directory works.

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 50 --num-requests 200

docs.title: Block Allocation Model
docs.text:
KV cache is allocated in blocks of the scenario pool's engine.block_size tokens. Each request consumes ceil(token_count / block_size) blocks. Blocks are reference-counted and can be shared across requests via prefix caching.

The GPU-tier block budget is not a flag. blis-latency-kernel computes it with its memory methods from the scenario — model, hardware, parallelism, quantization, cache_dtype, gpu_memory_utilization and block_size — per data-parallel rank: a pool with dp > 1 (MoE only) becomes one replica per rank, each with its own budget. A LoRA run's static adapter HBM reservation is set aside from that budget. To change the budget, change the scenario (for example its gpu_memory_utilization or cache_dtype).

Block size affects prefix cache granularity

Prefix caching uses block-aligned hashing (hash.ComputeBlockHashes). Smaller block sizes increase cache hit granularity but also increase allocation overhead. Choose block size relative to your typical prefix lengths.

docs.title: Prefix Caching
docs.text:
When requests share common prefixes (e.g., system prompts in RAG), BLIS can reuse KV cache blocks from prior computations. This reduces prefill tokens and improves TTFT.

Each instance reuses cached blocks on its own. Whether same-prefix requests land on the same instance is the llm-d router's decision. Its built-in default configuration includes the prefix-cache-scorer (weight 3, beside queue-scorer and kv-cache-utilization-scorer at 2), which estimates each endpoint's cached prefix from the requests the router has sent it; see Routing. examples/llm-d/prefix-affinity.yaml is an explicit prefix-aware configuration:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node-prefix-affinity.yaml \
  --scenarios examples/llm-d/scenarios --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 \
  --prefix-tokens 512 --rate 100 --num-requests 500

The precise-prefix-cache-producer, which reads vLLM KV-cache events, is refused: the simulated engines do not publish KV events.

docs.title: Disabling reuse across requests
docs.text:
A deployment launched with vLLM's --no-enable-prefix-caching reuses nothing across requests. A scenario states that with enable_prefix_caching: false on its pool's engine block; the field is tri-state, and omitting it takes vLLM's own default, which is on.

The setting changes the work a prefill does, not only the memory it holds: with reuse on, a matched prefix arrives as already-computed tokens and only the remainder is charged. A request's own progress is unaffected either way — a chunked prefill resumes from where it stopped, because that is not another request's block.

pools:
  - role: colocated
    engine:
      enable_prefix_caching: false

A workload whose requests share no prefix is unaffected by the setting, because there is nothing to reuse. That is the case for the AISimulate accuracy corpus, whose spec sets cached_prefix_tokens to zero.

docs.title: Minimum KV Block Requirements
docs.text:
DroppedUnservable rejection

Requests are dropped as unservable (incrementing DroppedUnservable) in two cases:

  1. MaxModelLen guard — requests whose total sequence length (input + output budget) exceeds the scenario's max_model_len are rejected before entering the queue. This mirrors vLLM's --max-model-len validation.
  2. KV capacity guard — when ceil(inputTokens / blockSize) > TotalCapacity(), the request physically cannot fit in GPU memory. This mirrors vLLM's pre-engine rejection path.

Both guards fire at enqueue time, before the request enters the wait queue.

Proactive MaxModelLen cap

A three-part enforcement of the scenario's max_model_len matches vLLM's scheduler semantics: (1) FormBatch proactively clamps token scheduling to maxModelLen - 1 - ProgressIndex, (2) executeBatchStep skips decode when no tokens are allocated, and (3) processCompletions force-completes requests at the maxModelLen - 1 boundary. Output per length-capped request: maxModelLen - inputLen tokens — ProgressIndex is BLIS's num_computed_tokens and lags the generated-token count by one (the first output token is charged to prefill), so stopping at maxModelLen - 1 is exactly vLLM's check_stop (num_tokens >= max_model_len) and the boundary token is counted.

Compute the minimum blocks needed for your workload:

min_blocks = ceil(max_input_tokens / block_size)

For a workload with max 7,000 input tokens and block size 16: ceil(7000/16) = 438 blocks minimum. Below this, requests are dropped. Below ~2x this threshold, cascading preemptions cause severe throughput degradation.

docs.title: Tiered Caching (GPU + CPU Offload)
docs.text:
The legacy single CPU tier is enabled with --kv-cpu-blocks:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --kv-cpu-blocks 50000 \
  --kv-offload-threshold 0.9 \
  --rate 100 --num-requests 500
Flag Default Description --kv-cpu-blocks 0 CPU-tier blocks (0 = disabled) --kv-offload-threshold 0.9 GPU utilization fraction above which blocks offload to CPU

The GPU↔CPU transfer is priced by the kernel from the catalog's cpu_dram storage device (<catalog>/devices/storage.yaml). There are no transfer-rate flags. For a multi-tier hierarchy, use --kv-offload-config instead; the two are mutually exclusive.

docs.title: Multi-Tier Offload Config Surface (--kv-offload-config)
docs.text:
The scalar flags above cover the single CPU tier. For vLLM's multi-tier offload (CPU → disk / object store), BLIS captures the full config surface through one strict-YAML file — --kv-offload-config <path> — with a single top-level kv_offload: block. This mirrors --lora-config / --saturation-config: absent ⇒ the offload subsystem is inert and output is byte-identical to a build without it.

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --kv-offload-config offload.yaml

kv_offload:
  cpu_bytes_to_use: 17179869184     # required when the block is present
  block_size: 16                    # optional; default = GPU block size (mutually
                                    #   exclusive with blocks_per_chunk)
  # blocks_per_chunk: 1             # alternate encoding of block_size (default 1); > 1 coalesces
                                    #   GPU blocks into offload chunks (INV-K6)
  eviction_policy: lru              # lru only (vLLM's arc is not simulated yet)
  offload_prompt_only: true         # vLLM DEFAULT (prompt-only). false => promptAndDecode:
                                    #   full decode blocks are offloaded and reused too (see below)
  # self_describing_kv_events: false
  # tokens_per_hash: 16             # default = GPU block size
  secondary_tiers:
    - type: fs                      # only "fs" is representable today; obj/p2p error loudly
      root_dir: /mnt/kv-cache
      n_read_threads: 16            # vLLM default 16
      n_write_threads: 16           # vLLM default 16
      locality: LOCAL               # LOCAL | REMOTE (optional)
      direct_io: true               # REQUIRED — BLIS makes vLLM's runtime O_DIRECT probe explicit;
                                    #   false (buffered I/O) is refused: not priced yet
      device_class: nvme_gen4       # REQUIRED — a catalog storage device; the kernel prices transfers

Defaults match vLLM knob-for-knob. Anything vLLM accepts either maps to a BLIS config or fails loudly at startup — never silently ignored: store_threshold >= 2 is rejected (vLLM's TieringOffloadingSpec rejects it), and obj/p2p/example tier types are rejected (no faithful BLIS mapping yet).

Every tier must name a device_class from the catalog's storage-device table (<catalog>/devices/storage.yaml, located by --catalog / BLIS_CATALOG); the kernel prices each tier transfer from that device (its TierTime). An explicit read_bandwidth, write_bandwidth or base_latency on a tier is refused. A catalog device's rates are O_DIRECT rates, so a tier with direct_io: false -- vLLM's buffered fallback on filesystems that reject O_DIRECT, such as overlayfs -- is refused too, until the kernel prices that regime (blis-latency-kernel#41). A class the catalog does not define, or a missing/malformed table, is a hard error naming the path. Under P/D disaggregation each pool sizes the tiers by its own bytes per block and prices them with its own kernel. A scenario's own offload block is the deployment's tier configuration (#1910): its cpu_dram tier is the CPU tier, and --kv-offload-config may only restate it (a disagreement is refused, naming the fields). See Latency models for the mapping and what it refuses.

Chunks (blocks_per_chunk, INV-K6). The tiers hold vLLM's offload chunks: blocks_per_chunk GPU blocks keyed by their last block's hash. The CPU tier holds cpu_bytes_to_use // (bytes per block × blocks_per_chunk) chunks, evicts whole chunks in LRU order, and every tier transfer moves one chunk. A load starts at the chunk holding the GPU-cached boundary, covers whole chunks, and is skipped when it is shorter than one chunk. A store offers whole prompt chunks only. A CPU budget under one chunk is refused at startup. blis-schemas' offload block cannot yet state the width (the proposed field is offload.blocks_per_chunk), so --kv-offload-config supplies it beside a scenario block. Every other field must still agree.

The resolved config is recorded in the exported trace header, so a blis run --trace-output round-trips through blis replay (INV-13): on replay the header is authoritative and a config the binary cannot reproduce fails loudly rather than silently degrading to single-tier.

The offload_prompt_only knob is an explicit policy over what enters the tiers. Modeling vLLM's mechanism (_calc_num_offloadable_tokens + storable_chunks), a request's computed KV is truncated to the prompt length when true (the default), then floor-divided into whole chunks — so a chunk containing any decode token is never offloaded (a prompt of 1.5 × the chunk size offloads exactly 1 chunk). With offload_prompt_only: false (vLLM's promptAndDecode), full decode blocks are offloaded too; because BLIS already hashes every completed block prefix-consistently (for block_size > 1), a later request on the same instance whose input contains earlier output tokens (multi-turn / agentic workloads) reloads that decode KV from the tiers instead of recomputing it. A reloaded prefix is billed as a cache hit — its tokens are dropped from the prefill forward pass, so it lowers that request's prefill compute and TTFT rather than being charged as a full recompute (#1699; the same correction applies to the legacy --kv-cpu-blocks tier). Reuse is single-instance (offload tiers are per-instance and invisible to the router).

At block_size == 1 decode blocks take a guarded allocation path that leaves them unhashed, so decode-offload is inert there — a degenerate offload block size (real offload block sizes track the GPU block size). With no --kv-offload-config, behavior is unchanged (INV-6).

docs.title: Enabling and Disabling Offload
docs.text: Offload is off by default. There is one switch — the presence of --kv-offload-config (or, for the legacy tier, a non-zero --kv-cpu-blocks). The two are mutually exclusive.

docs.title: Sizing the CPU Tier
docs.text:
The CPU tier is configured in bytes, but the cache uses it in blocks — the same unit as the GPU tier. BLIS converts once, at startup:

block_capacity = floor(cpu_bytes_to_use / per_block_bytes)

per_block_bytes is derived from the model, so it differs per deployment. The rule that matters: block_capacity must comfortably exceed the GPU-tier budget. A CPU tier no larger than the GPU tier cannot serve anything the GPU evicted, and the run will show no benefit.

Offload also only helps if blocks are evicted from the GPU and later requested again — for example a workload with many distinct per-tenant prefixes (prefix_sharing: per_member) whose working set exceeds the GPU tier. Note that a workload spec's prefix_length is added to the sampled input_distribution length, not carved out of it.

cpu_bytes_to_use is per GPU, not per deployment

Under tensor parallelism the KV cache is sharded across ranks, so both sides of that division are per-rank quantities. The host memory a deployment actually consumes is TP × cpu_bytes_to_use. A node-level memory budget must therefore be divided by TP before it goes in the file. This matches vLLM, where cpu_bytes_to_use is likewise a per-worker budget.

docs.title: Chunked Prefill
docs.text:
Long prefill sequences can cause head-of-line (HOL) blocking — a long prefill occupies a whole step, blocking shorter requests from starting.

Chunked prefill splits long prefills into smaller chunks:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --long-prefill-token-threshold 256 \
  --rate 100 --num-requests 500

Chunked prefill benefits TTFT, not ITL

With --long-prefill-token-threshold=256, short-request TTFT p99 improves by ~52% in bimodal workloads. But ITL is unaffected (<0.5%) because ~255 of ~256 ITL samples per request are decode-only steps. The benefit is in scheduling new requests, not in token generation speed.

A lone request is not chunked

As in vLLM v0.31.0 (#57951), the threshold applies only when the engine's scheduler holds another request, running or waiting. A request alone takes the whole max_num_batched_tokens budget, since there is nobody for it to starve.

docs.title: Batch Formation Parameters
docs.text: KV cache pressure is directly coupled to batch formation. The scenario pool's engine.max_num_seqs (maximum requests in the running batch) and engine.max_num_batched_tokens (token budget per step) are the primary capacity knobs, with vLLM's meaning. Reducing them decreases KV cache pressure but also reduces throughput.

docs.title: Identifying the KV Pressure Cliff
docs.text:
Preemption rates spike non-linearly once the working set exceeds the KV budget. Sweep offered load against a fixed scenario to find it:

for rate in 5 10 20 40 80; do
  echo "=== rate=$rate ==="
  ./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
    --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
    --rate $rate --num-requests 200 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -E "preemption_count|completed_requests"
done

Distribution median drives KV pressure

ParetoLogNormal distributions produce fewer preemptions than Gaussian despite similar means, because the Pareto component's median (~79 tokens) is much lower than Gaussian's median (~256 tokens). Short requests cycle faster, creating "breathing room" in the KV cache.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Core Engine: KV Cache — internal mechanics
  • Configuration Reference — all KV cache flags
  • Metrics & Results — understanding preemption rate, cache hit rate, KV thrashing

docs.title: KV Cache Hit-Rate Calibration
docs.text:
Deprecated workflow

blis observe and blis calibrate are deprecated (#1901). blis replay is not. This page is kept for existing users of the pipeline.

This note documents how to validate BLIS's tiered KV-offload model against real vLLM runs using the observe → replay → calibrate pipeline (issue #1583, part of the multi-tier KV-offload epic #1585). It complements Observe / Replay / Calibrate and KV Cache & Memory.

docs.title: What gets compared
docs.text:
blis calibrate compares TTFT, E2E, and — as of #1583 — the KV cache hit-rate:

  • Real hit-rate is scraped from the vLLM server's Prometheus /metrics endpoint by blis observe --scrape-kv-metrics and recorded in the trace header (observed_kv_metrics).
  • Simulated hit-rate is read from the blis replay --metrics-path MetricsOutput file: cache_hit_rate (the GPU prefix cache's prompt-token rate) against a GPU-cache observation, cache_hit_rate + cpu_tier_hit_rate (tokens either tier served) against a tiered one.
  • blis calibrate --sim-metrics <that file> reports the absolute error in percentage points and a pass/fail verdict against --hit-rate-tolerance-pp (default 5 pp), plus a TTFT-MAPE verdict against --ttft-mape-threshold (default 0.15).

Against a tiered observation the comparison is on the overall hit-rate (both tiers). Per-tier read/write time is recorded in the header (read_time_total / write_time_total) as informational data for a manual bandwidth cross-check — the simulator has no per-tier hit counters to compare against.

docs.title: Dependency on an unreleased vLLM
docs.text:
The tiered counters vllm:kv_offload_tiering_block_hits / vllm:kv_offload_tiering_block_queries (and ..._read_time / ..._write_time) come from vLLM PR #48798, which is in no release tag. Record the exact commit the cluster ran with --vllm-commit <sha> — it is stored verbatim in the header so the dependency is explicit and reproducible.

If the server exposes only released metrics, --scrape-kv-metrics falls back to the GPU-only vllm:gpu_prefix_cache_* family and tags the observation source: gpu-prefix-cache-fallback. This is a weaker validation (GPU tier only, no offload tiers) and is never conflated with a tiered hit-rate — treat it as a separate, weaker check.

docs.title: Minimal experiment set
docs.text:
Validate against the four canonical cache paths, over a small prefix-length sweep, single replica:

Path How to elicit it GPU hit Repeat a prompt whose prefix is still resident in the GPU KV cache. CPU hit Repeat a prefix that has been offloaded to the CPU staging tier but evicted from GPU. Storage hit Repeat a prefix that has cascaded to a secondary fs tier and been evicted from CPU. Full miss A unique prefix with no cached blocks anywhere.

Sweep the shared prefix length (e.g. 256 / 1024 / 4096 tokens) so the hit-rate spans its range. Keep the deployment to a single replica so the aggregate hit-rate is unambiguous; the replay scenario must state the same model, hardware and parallelism as the observed server.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
# 1. Observe the real server, scraping the per-tier counters into the trace header.
#    --vllm-commit records the pinned (unreleased) vLLM the counters require. observe
#    dispatches to a real server and does not itself model the offload tiers, so no
#    --kv-offload-config is passed here — the observed hit-rate is whatever the server
#    reports.
blis observe --server-url http://localhost:8000 --model <model> \
  --workload-spec sweep.yaml \
  --scrape-kv-metrics --vllm-commit <sha> \
  --trace-header t.yaml --trace-data t.csv

# 2. Replay the captured trace through the DES to produce the SIM-side hit-rate. Supply
#    --kv-offload-config matching the observed deployment — replay models the tiers and
#    derives the aggregate cache_hit_rate into --metrics-path. Each tier must name a
#    catalog device_class. (A tiered observation
#    replayed WITHOUT an offload config is a hard error, never a silent GPU-only value.)
blis replay --trace-header t.yaml --trace-data t.csv \
  --scenario <scenario.yaml> --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry <blis-registry> \
  --kv-offload-config offload.yaml \
  --results-path sim.json --metrics-path simagg.json

# 3. Compare. TTFT/E2E come from --sim-results; the hit-rate comes from --sim-metrics.
blis calibrate --trace-header t.yaml --trace-data t.csv \
  --sim-results sim.json --sim-metrics simagg.json \
  --hit-rate-tolerance-pp 5 --ttft-mape-threshold 0.15 \
  --report calibration.json

Note. blis observe records the observed hit-rate and its source, but not the offload config — it is a black-box dispatcher against a real server. The operator supplies the deployment's --kv-offload-config on the replay step so the simulator reproduces the tiered behaviour. For a sim-generated trace (blis run --kv-offload-config … --trace-output) the config is instead recorded in the header and reproduced authoritatively on replay (INV-13).

The report's hit_rate block reports real_hit_rate, sim_hit_rate, abs_error_pp, tolerance_pp, within, and source. Targets on the minimal set: TTFT MAPE ≤ 15% and hit-rate absolute error ≤ 5 pp.

docs.title: Notes and caveats
docs.text:
• The counter delta spans the whole measured window, which includes any warm-up requests (they are excluded from TTFT/E2E calibration but not from the engine-level counter delta). Keep warm-up small, or prefer --prewarm-duration (which runs before the start scrape).
  • A scrape miss (unreachable /metrics, no recognized counters, zero queries, or a counter reset mid-window) is not fatal: observe warns and omits observed_kv_metrics; the workload trace is still exported.
  • The read_time/write_time counters are vLLM device service time excluding queue wait — they calibrate the offload tiers' service term, not the queueing term. Do not fit queue wait against them.

docs.title: Latency Models
docs.text: BLIS takes its latency model from one source: blis-latency-kernel (Go module github.com/inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel, pinned at v0.3.0). The adapter in sim/kernelmodel translates a BLIS batch into the kernel's request shapes and converts the kernel's answers to BLIS ticks; it computes no cost of its own. There is no other backend and no --latency-model flag: the roofline and trained-physics backends, the alpha/beta coefficients, hardware_config.json calibration, and the trained_physics_coefficients block of defaults.yaml were removed.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text: inference-sim simulates the cluster: arrivals, admission, routing, scheduling, KV block accounting, placement and metrics. blis-latency-kernel prices: step time, KV and fixed memory, P/D KV transfer, offload tier transfer and host overheads. It reads model graphs, chips, fabrics and storage devices from blis-catalog and fitted coefficients from blis-registry; every file format involved, the scenario included, is defined by blis-schemas. See The BLIS repositories.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
git clone --branch 0.3.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-catalog.git
git clone --branch v0.2.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry.git
export BLIS_CATALOG=$PWD/blis-catalog
./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 10 --num-requests 100

The pinned releases are explained in Catalog compatibility.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Four roots, all required on blis run and blis replay:

input what it names --scenario a scenario file name inside --scenarios --scenarios a directory of scenario YAML files --registry a blis-registry clone root, holding the coefficient sets a scenario names --catalog / BLIS_CATALOG a blis-catalog clone root

A scenario directory can be any directory of scenario YAMLs. The kernel module ships the scenarios it was scored on, at $(go env GOMODCACHE)/github.com/inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel@v0.3.0/testdata/aisimulate (after go mod download). This repo's own fixtures are in testdata/scenarios/: glm-5-h200-3p1d-ib.yaml (P/D) and glm-5-h200-tp8-mtp3.yaml (MTP speculation).

docs.title: Scenario structure
docs.text:
A scenario is a blis-schemas file of two YAML documents, a Scenario and a Deployment:

kind: Scenario
name: llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4
engine_version: "0.29.0"
model: llama-3.1-70b-instruct
coefficients: [cost-model-primitives, cost-model-collectives, cost-model-host-overheads,
               cost-model-attention, cost-model-recurrent, cost-model-memory]
cluster:
  hardware: h200
  nodes: 1
  gpus_per_node: 8
  # fabric: ib-400g      # the inter-node fabric, needed when a handoff crosses nodes
---
kind: Deployment
name: llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4
pools:
  - role: colocated        # colocated | prefill | decode
    nodes: 1
    parallel: {tp: 4, pp: 1, dp: 1, enable_expert_parallel: false}
    engine:
      quantization: fp8
      cache_dtype: fp8
      block_size: 16
      max_num_batched_tokens: 8192
      max_num_seqs: 256
      max_model_len: 32768   # required
      cudagraph_mode: PIECEWISE
      gpu_memory_utilization: 0.9
      # enable_prefix_caching: false
      # speculative: {method: mtp, num_spec_tokens: 3}
# offload: ...               # optional
# pd_transfer: {connector: NixlConnector}   # optional, P/D scenarios

docs.title: What comes from the scenario, and what stays on the CLI
docs.text:
The scenario and the kernel supply, with no flag to restate them: the model, the hardware, TP/DP/EP, the KV block budget (from the kernel's memory methods, per data-parallel rank), block size, max_num_seqs, max_num_batched_tokens, max_model_len (a count is kept; unstated takes the model graph's context window; auto or -1 takes that window shrunk to what one rank's KV cache holds, as vLLM v0.31.0 starts; a window one rank cannot hold, or none at all, is refused), prefix caching, the KV cache dtype, and the speculative draft length and method. The flags that used to state these (--model, --hardware, --tp, --dp, --total-kv-blocks, --max-num-seqs, --max-model-len, --kv-cache-dtype, --num-speculative-tokens, ...) no longer exist; to change one, edit the scenario.

Everything a scenario does not state stays on the command line: the workload, rate and concurrency, routing, admission, scheduling, flow control, saturation detectors, the instance count and P/D topology, LoRA, KV offload tiers, and seed/horizon/output flags. See the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: What the kernel prices
docs.text:
• Step time. One forward pass over the scheduled batch, composed from per-operator costs (GEMMs, attention, grouped expert GEMMs, recurrent state updates, collectives, elementwise and host terms) with coefficients fitted against vendor kernel sweeps. BLIS reads the kernel's no-overlap edge of the band it reports. Expert geometry comes from the model graph in the catalog, not from an HF config.
  • Memory. Weights, fixed overheads and the per-block KV cost, from which BLIS takes the KV block budget for each data-parallel rank.
  • Host overheads. Per-request queueing (tokenization and preprocessing), per-output-token processing, and the fixed per-request completion overhead. The per-request admission overhead runs on the endpoint's API-server render threads, in arrival order (INV-R1): --renderer-num-workers threads (vLLM's renderer_num_workers, default 1) on each of --api-server-count servers (default: vLLM's per-mode count -- dp behind an internal or hybrid DP replica, else 1). Under a burst, requests therefore queue for the tokenizer. blis-schemas does not yet state either setting; the proposed fields are engine.renderer_num_workers and parallel.api_server_count.
  • P/D KV transfer and offload tier transfer, below.

A scenario that cannot be resolved -- absent file, unreadable coefficient set, unknown engine version, a deployment that does not fit -- aborts the run naming what failed. There is no fallback.

docs.title: Prefill/decode disaggregation
docs.text:
A scenario with a prefill pool and a decode pool, run with --prefill-instances and --decode-instances. BLIS builds one kernel per pool, so each pool is priced at its own parallelism and engine settings. The KV handoff from a prefill instance to a decode instance is priced by the kernel's PDTransferTime over the scenario's fabric, between the two instances' placements (NVLink when they share a node). Each instance count must not exceed its pool's rank capacity: pool nodes × gpus_per_node / (pp × tp × pcp).

Refused: a P/D topology over a colocated scenario; a disaggregated scenario run without --prefill-instances/--decode-instances; pools that differ in block size, dp or draft configuration; a handoff connector other than NIXL's; shared (--prefill-decode-instances) or encode instances.

The handoff follows vLLM v0.31.0's NIXL protocol, so the scenario's pd_transfer.connector must be NixlConnector, NixlPullConnector, NixlPushConnector or a MultiConnector over one; any other connector is refused. Three further rules follow from vLLM:

  • An offload tier needs a MultiConnector. With a tier, pd_transfer.connector must be MultiConnector: setting kv_offloading_size replaces kv_connector with the OffloadingConnector (vllm/config/vllm.py:1124-1158), so a plain NIXL connector and a tier cannot run together.
  • A MultiConnector is assumed to list NixlConnector first. The first connector in config order that reports tokens loads them (multi_connector.py:134-141, 429-448). blis-schemas states neither the children nor their order, so BLIS assumes llm-d's composition and says so on stderr.

  • A model whose NIXL prefill backs off is refused. That covers Mamba-state models and multi-module MTP drafting K > 1: the decode side recomputes the trailing prompt tokens (_prefill_backoff, nixl/base_scheduler.py:385-407), which BLIS does not model. DSpark backs off nothing: its prefill lookahead is 1 (config/vllm.py:657-678).

  • Decode-side load (INV-PD-8). The decode instance takes its own prefix-cache hit first (whole blocks, never the prompt's last token) and reserves the rest (WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS). The handoff moves and is priced for only those blocks, so a session's later turn on the same decode instance pulls only its new blocks.

  • Prefill KV hold (INV-PD-7). The prefill instance keeps a finished request's blocks, which count against its KV capacity, until the pull completes. They are freed at once if the decode side never took the request, and at NIXL's 30 s lease expiry if the decode instance went away mid-pull.
  • Contention (INV-P2-2, --pd-transfer-contention, default off). Concurrent handoffs share the links they cross. The links come from the kernel's PDTransferDemand: the sender's NIC egress and the receiver's NIC ingress across nodes, or the NVLink domain on one node. Each link is divided max-min fairly and re-divided as handoffs start and finish. The floor is never shared. A handoff alone still takes exactly PDTransferTime. With contention off, every handoff is priced as if alone.
  • Offload tiers (#1940). The scenario's offload block (or --kv-offload-config, see KV offload) gives every pool its own tier of that size: llm-d's MultiConnector of NIXL and the OffloadingConnector. A pool's tier stores what its engine computes. The prefill pool's tier serves prefix hits before compute. The decode pool's tier serves the requests the decode pool runs itself (those the decider does not disaggregate), but never a remotely prefilled prompt, which NIXL, listed first, loads. A 0-byte tier is refused, as vLLM refuses it.

The PD section on stdout, and the results file's pd block, report the handoffs, their p50 and p90 durations, the queueing delay contention added (duration minus the uncontended price), each link's peak concurrent handoffs, the prefill KV hold's peak, and each pool's CPU-tier hit rate.

docs.title: Data and expert parallelism (MoE)
docs.text:
With dp > 1 BLIS runs one engine per data-parallel rank, each sized as one EngineCore (the kernel's per-rank KV budget and caps). enable_expert_parallel is priced by the kernel. A dense model with dp > 1 is refused.

Lockstep (#1909). The dp ranks of one logical instance are one vLLM DP group. vLLM v0.31.0 runs an MoE model at dp > 1 as DPEngineCoreProc ranks (vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1386-1395), with or without expert parallelism: use_all2all is true at dp > 1 (vllm/config/parallel.py:738-743), so every MoE layer is a collective over the ranks. BLIS therefore steps the group's ranks together:

  • Every rank runs every step. A rank with nothing ready runs vLLM's dummy batch, one uniform decode of 1 + num_spec_tokens tokens (execute_dummy_batch, core.py:2280-2287; vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:1376-1382).
  • Each rank is priced by the kernel at its own batch padded to the group's largest token count, when that count is within the CUDA-graph capture ceiling the kernel resolved (coordinate_batch_across_dp, vllm/v1/worker/dp_utils.py:99-181: ranks pad only when the synced graph mode is not NONE). Past the ceiling, under FULL_DECODE_ONLY with a mixed batch, or when the layout runs no graphs, each rank costs its own batch. The ceiling and the graph modes come from the kernel; a layout that runs graphs with no readable ceiling is refused at startup rather than priced unpadded.
  • The step lasts the slowest rank's price, plus that rank's own offload reload time, and every rank's clock advances by it. Requests that reach any rank at a step's own tick (arrival, queueing, adapter load) join that step, whichever rank they are on.
  • The wave ends only when the unfinished-request all-reduce finds every rank idle. That all-reduce runs on the wave's first step and every 16th (dp_sync_interval, vllm/config/parallel.py:150; core.py:2333-2350), so up to 15 dummy steps follow the last request. Dummy steps are not work: a rank's clock, and so SimEndedTime and the rates divided by it, stop at its last real event.

How requests reach ranks: parallel.data_parallel_load_balancing (or --dp-load-balancing, which may only restate a mode the scenario states). vLLM v0.31.0's serve flags choose (vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:536-538, 1225-1242; EngineCoreClient.make_async_mp_client, vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py:155-166), and lockstep is the same in every mode:

mode vLLM router sees internal (default) no LB flag: one front-end balances all ranks (DPLBAsyncMPClient) one endpoint per replica (below) hybrid --data-parallel-hybrid-lb: one front-end per node balances that node's ranks the same, for a replica on one node; a replica across nodes is refused external --data-parallel-external-lb or --data-parallel-multi-port-external-lb: every rank serves its own port (DPAsyncMPClient) every rank, with its own signals and its own prefix cache; the router picks the rank

One endpoint per replica (internal, hybrid). The router sees each DP group as one pod, listed under its rank 0 instance ID; a request routed to it is assigned to a rank by vLLM v0.31.0's internal DP load balancer (DPLBAsyncMPClient.get_core_engine_for_request, vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py:1589-1640): the rank with the lowest max(client_count x in_flight, waiting + running), plus waiting x 6 x max(0, kv_usage - 0.5) when anything waits, over the per-rank counts the DP coordinator publishes every 100 ms (vllm/v1/engine/coordinator.py:154-162). Between publishes the chosen rank's waiting count is bumped and the scan start rotates, as the front-end does; in_flight is the front-end's exact count of its unfinished requests per rank. The endpoint's signals follow how llm-d's endpoint picker reads a pod's per-engine series (engine="<rank>" labels, vllm/v1/metrics/loggers.py:480-486):

signal endpoint value queue depth, running batch, in-flight requests, KV tokens and capacity sum over ranks KV utilization max over ranks (llm-d-router#3085; v0.10.0 read rank 0's series alone) prefix cache (precise scorer) rank 0's cache only

The prefix-cache view is rank 0's because vLLM publishes each rank's KV events on base + rank (vllm/distributed/kv_events.py:355-356) and llm-d subscribes an endpoint at the pool port plus its rank index (pkg/kvevents/pool.go:134), which is 0 for an internal-balancer pod.

Known deviations and limits:

  • Pad tokens are the kernel's Batch.PadTokens (blis-schemas#74): they run the GEMMs, collectives, MoE dispatch and experts, and no attention, logits or sampling; an idle rank's dummy batch is all pad. This needs the kernel and schemas from the dsv41 branches, which go.mod pins by replace until they are released.
  • vLLM also pads every rank under dual-batch overlap (should_ubatch, dp_utils.py:181). BLIS does not model DBO, which the kernel does not price (blis-latency-kernel#48).
  • One front-end, with the whole in-flight view, stands for the api_server_count front-ends (dp by default), so client_count is 1.
  • The coordinator's counts are sampled at the first assignment of each 100 ms period, not at the publish instant.
  • A P/D pool's ranks step in lockstep but stay individually routable.
  • The autoscaler is still refused with dp > 1, and a rank whose startup placement is deferred refuses the run.

docs.title: Speculative Decoding / MTP (#1528)
docs.text: A pool that states engine.speculative: {method, num_spec_tokens} drafts K tokens per step. BLIS does not predict acceptance, since it runs no draft model: it resolves it (below).

docs.title: Speculative acceptance (#1939)
docs.text:
The acceptance length AL (tokens per verification step, counting the bonus token, in [1, K+1]; rate α = (AL − 1)/K) is resolved by blis-schemas' acceptance.Resolve from the highest layer that states it, lowest to highest:
