Note: hypothesis scripts written before BC-14 may divide scheduling_delay_ms by 1,000 unnecessarily — that field is now already in ms.

docs.title: Scenario Overrides
docs.text:
A run reproduces its scenario unless a flag or a policy bundle chooses another value for a setting the scenario states. Today those are the two settings vLLM's engine.scheduling_policy decides: the waiting queue's order and the preemption victim (vLLM fcfs is BLIS --scheduler fcfs with --preemption-policy fcfs; vLLM priority is --scheduler priority-fcfs with --preemption-policy priority). An explicit --scheduler or --preemption-policy, or a --policy-config bundle's scheduler or preemption.policy, that differs from the scenario is kept, since exploring a policy against a fixed deployment is the point, and the results file says so:

{
  "overrides": [
    {"setting": "scheduler", "scenario": "priority-fcfs", "run": "sjf", "source": "--scheduler"}
  ]
}

In a prefill/decode deployment each pool runs its own engine's policy, so a run-level choice is recorded once per pool whose engine stated otherwise, as "scheduler (prefill pool)" or "preemption_policy (decode pool)".

A warning on stderr says the same. Like catalog, the block is file-only.

docs.title: Catalog Provenance
docs.text:
The catalog field records which model catalog produced the result (#1732), so a results file is attributable and an experiment is distinguishable from a reproducible run. It is written by both blis run --metrics-path and blis replay --metrics-path:

{
  "catalog": {
    "path": "/home/me/blis-catalog",
    "revision": "63a9a5010a3f0c1d9f6b2e4a7c8d5b1e2f3a4b5c",
    "dirty": false
  }
}
  • path — the catalog clone root that was located by --catalog / BLIS_CATALOG, recorded verbatim as supplied: a relative value stays relative and an absolute value stays absolute, neither is rewritten. So the field is not categorically CWD-relative — a relative value is only interpretable alongside the working directory the run was launched from, which is a reason to prefer an absolute --catalog / BLIS_CATALOG when the results file needs to be attributable later.
  • revision — the catalog's git commit, or "unknown" when the catalog is not a git checkout (a revision is never invented).
  • dirty — true when the catalog subtree has uncommitted or untracked content, i.e. the run used a config the recorded revision does not contain. A catalog inside a larger repository is judged on its own subtree, so an unrelated edit elsewhere in that repository does not mark the run an experiment. dirty is always false alongside an unknown revision — there is no committed state to differ from.

File-only, by design

Provenance appears only in the --metrics-path file, never on stdout. Catalog git state legitimately differs between two otherwise identical runs, and stdout is the byte-identical channel INV-6 protects. A run without --metrics-path never consults git at all — and a results file written by a run whose catalog could not be resolved simply omits the block.

docs.title: Saturation Detection
docs.text:
Post-hoc saturation analysis classifies a completed run as STABLE, BACKLOGGED or OVERLOADED. It is distinct from the llm-d router's saturation detector, which gates admission and flow control during the run. Select detectors with --detectors <name|comma-list|all> (composite, threshold, backlog-drift, peak-rate), tune them with --saturation-config, and write the per-event verdict trace with --saturation-report:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 10 --num-requests 100 --detectors all --saturation-report sat.json

Detector mechanics and tuning knobs: Saturation analyzer.

docs.title: Per-Request Fields
docs.text:
When the requests array is non-empty, each entry contains:

Field Unit Description requestID string Unique request identifier arrived_at s Arrival timestamp in simulation seconds (ArrivalTime / 1,000,000) num_prefill_tokens count Input (prompt) token count num_decode_tokens count Output token count ttft_ms ms Time To First Token for this request itl_ms ms Mean Inter-Token Latency for this request e2e_ms ms End-to-End latency for this request scheduling_delay_ms ms Time spent in the wait queue before first scheduling slo_class string SLO class (critical, standard, batch, etc.) — omitted if empty tenant_id string Tenant label — omitted if empty handled_by string Instance ID that processed the request — omitted if empty model string Model tag — omitted if empty length_capped bool true if request was force-completed at MaxModelLen — omitted when false gateway_queue_delay_ms ms Time from the router enqueuing the request in flow control to its dispatch — omitted when flow control (featureGates: [flowControl]) is off session_id string Multi-turn session link — omitted for single-turn requests round_index int Round within session (0 = first turn); always present, defaults to 0 for non-session requests

docs.title: Anomaly Counters
docs.text:
When anomalies are detected, BLIS prints === Anomaly Counters ===:

Counter What It Means Action Priority Inversions A lower-priority request was scheduled before a higher-priority one Check scheduler choice — use priority-fcfs for SLO workloads HOL Blocking Events A long prefill blocked shorter requests Enable chunked prefill: --long-prefill-token-threshold 256 Rejected Requests (Admission) The llm-d router denied admission: an admitter plugin, or the legacy admission controller shedding a sheddable request (priority < 0) from a saturated pool Check the InferenceObjective priorities and the saturation detector's parameters; see Admission Control Shed (tier) Per-SLO-class count of requests the router shed (admission denials and flow-control TTL expiries) — printed as indented sub-items beneath Rejected Requests (Admission) Raise the class's InferenceObjective priority, or the detector's thresholds Rejected Requests (Routing) No endpoint could serve the request: no ready candidates (all instances Loading or Draining), or every filter eliminated all Increase initial_nodes, reduce loading_delay.mean, stagger drain operations, or check the router configuration's filters Dropped Unservable Request exceeds the context window (the scenario's max_model_len) or needs more KV blocks than exist Check the scenario's max_model_len; deploy more GPUs per instance or reduce max input tokens Timed Out Requests Request exceeded its client deadline before completing Increase --timeout or reduce load Length-Capped Requests Request was force-completed when it reached MaxModelLen tokens during decode Expected if workloads push against the scenario's max_model_len Gateway Queue Depth (horizon) Requests still waiting in the router's flow control when the simulation ended — printed only when > 0 Reduce arrival rate or increase cluster capacity Gateway Queue Rejected Requests flow control rejected because its queues were at capacity — printed only when > 0 Raise flowControl.maxRequests or the priority band's capacity in the EndpointPickerConfig Gateway Expired (TTL) Requests that waited in flow control past their queue-wait budget — printed only when > 0 Raise flowControl.defaultRequestTTL, or add capacity Encode Routing Rejections Requests rejected at an encode stage — printed only when > 0 —

Each counter is one INV-1 bucket; see Admission Control for how router outcomes map onto them.

Stdout-only vs JSON counters

Dropped Unservable, Timed Out Requests, and Length-Capped Requests also appear as fields in the --metrics-path JSON output (see Primary Metrics: dropped_unservable, timed_out_requests, length_capped_requests).

All other counters in this table — including Shed (tier), Gateway Queue Depth (horizon), and Gateway Queue Shed — are stdout-only and do not appear in the JSON file.

blis replay anomaly block

blis replay produces a subset of this output: Timed Out Requests, Gateway Queue Depth (horizon), and Gateway Queue Shed are currently missing from the blis replay anomaly block even when non-zero (tracked in issue #1184).

docs.title: KV Cache Metrics
docs.text:
When KV cache activity is nonzero, BLIS prints === KV Cache Metrics ===:

Metric Meaning Concern Threshold Preemption Rate Ratio of preemption events to completed requests — a single request can be preempted more than once > 5% indicates KV pressure Cache Hit Rate Fraction of blocks served from prefix cache Higher is better — indicates prefix reuse KV Thrashing Rate Repeated preemption-reallocation cycles > 0 indicates severe memory pressure

docs.title: Per-SLO-Class Metrics
docs.text: When multiple SLO classes are present in the workload, BLIS prints per-class TTFT and E2E distributions. This lets you verify that critical requests meet SLOs even when batch traffic is heavy.

docs.title: Per-Model Metrics
docs.text:
When instances serve different models (multi-model deployment), BLIS prints per-model TTFT mean/p99, E2E mean/p99, and throughput (req/s). This appears automatically when requests carry model tags. Output format:

=== Per-Model Metrics ===
  qwen/qwen3-14b:
    TTFT: p50=1234.56 p99=5678.90 (n=250)
    E2E:  p50=9876.54 p99=12345.67 (n=250)
    Throughput: 50.00 req/s, 6400.00 tok/s

Per-model metrics appear on stdout only. The --metrics-path JSON file (see Primary Metrics) contains only the aggregate MetricsOutput fields. The same applies to per-tenant, session, and PD metrics — all are stdout-only sections.

docs.title: Per-Tenant Metrics
docs.text:
When requests carry tenant_id labels, BLIS prints per-tenant request counts, total output tokens served, and a Jain Fairness Index over the token distribution. This section appears automatically and is omitted when no requests carry tenant labels (backward-compatible with legacy and untenanted workloads). A workload with a single named tenant shows the section with Jain=1.0 (trivially fair).

=== Per-Tenant Metrics ===
  alice: requests=50, tokens=12500
  bob: requests=50, tokens=12480
  Jain Fairness Index: 0.9999

Tenants are listed in lexicographic order. The Jain Fairness Index ranges from 1/N (maximally unfair — one tenant receives everything) to 1.0 (perfectly fair — all tenants receive equal tokens). A balanced two-tenant workload produces a value ≥ 0.99.

To tag requests with tenant labels, set tenant_id in your workload spec cohort:

cohorts:
  - name: alice-traffic
    tenant_id: alice
    ...
  - name: bob-traffic
    tenant_id: bob
    ...

docs.title: Session Metrics
docs.text:
When a workload contains multi-turn sessions (requests with session_id), BLIS prints a === Session Metrics === block:

Line What It Means Sessions Number of distinct multi-turn sessions in the workload TTFT cold (round 0) TTFT distribution for the first round of each session — no KV cache warmth from prior context TTFT warm (round≥1) TTFT distribution for follow-up rounds — benefits from cached context Session duration End-to-end duration from session start (first round arrival) to last round completion

Cold vs. warm TTFT split reveals prefix cache effectiveness: if TTFT warm ≈ TTFT cold, prefix caching is not activating for continuations — check that the router configuration includes the prefix-cache-scorer and that its weight is not dominated by load scorers.

docs.title: PD Disaggregation Metrics
docs.text:
When PD disaggregation is active (--prefill-instances > 0), BLIS prints a === PD Metrics === block:

Field What It Means Disaggregated Requests Requests that completed KV transfer through the prefill→decode path Dropped at Decode KV Requests whose transferred KV blocks could not be accepted by the decode instance Prefill Throughput Sub-request completion rate on prefill instances (sub-req/s) Decode Throughput Sub-request completion rate on decode instances (sub-req/s) Load Imbalance Ratio max(prefill_load, decode_load) / min(...) — 1.0 = perfectly balanced; inf = one pool has no completions Parent TTFT Client-visible TTFT (decode-sub-request scheduling delay + first decode step) — the arrival → first-token-emitted-by-decode span, including the decode-queue wait and exactly one output-token processing overhead (#1510); distribution in microseconds KV Transfer Duration Time to transfer KV blocks from prefill to decode instance, priced by blis-latency-kernel over the scenario's fabric; distribution in microseconds

PD Disaggregation Metrics are produced by both blis run and blis replay for a disaggregated scenario run with --prefill-instances/--decode-instances.

docs.title: Fitness Evaluation
docs.text:
For automated multi-configuration comparison:

--fitness-weights "p99_ttft:3,mean_e2e:1,throughput:2"

Valid metric keys: throughput, tokens_per_sec, p99_ttft, p50_ttft, mean_ttft, p99_e2e, p50_e2e, mean_e2e.

docs.title: How Normalization Works
docs.text:
• Latency metrics: 1 / (1 + value/1000) — lower latency → higher score. Reference: 1000 ticks = 1ms
  • Throughput metrics: value / (value + reference) — higher throughput → higher score. References: RPS=100, TPS=10,000

Normalization compresses large differences

The 1/(1+x/1000) function compresses large raw differences into small score differences. A 38% TTFT p99 improvement (39,000→64,000 ticks) maps to only 2-8% fitness score difference. Always examine raw metrics alongside fitness scores for meaningful comparison.

docs.title: Saturation Curves
docs.text: As arrival rate increases past per-instance service capacity (μ ≈ 1/step_time), TTFT p99 grows super-linearly. The queue growth rate excess = λ/k - μ determines how quickly latency degrades.

docs.title: Tail Latency Spikes
docs.text: P99 diverges from mean sharply near saturation. A workload at 90% capacity may show 2x mean TTFT but 10x P99 TTFT.

docs.title: Metrics Staleness Effects
docs.text: The router scores endpoints from metrics it scrapes every --refresh-metrics-interval (an EPP flag). Between scrapes it sees stale queue and KV-cache values, so load-only configurations can send bursts to the same endpoint. Shorten the interval in the scenario's router.epp_flags, or add a scorer fed by the router's own in-flight accounting (active-request-scorer), to reduce the effect.

docs.title: Configuration Equivalence at Low Load
docs.text: Router configurations produce near-equivalent results at low utilization. Differentiation requires moderate-to-high load where queueing dynamics dominate.

docs.title: Host Overhead
docs.text: blis-latency-kernel prices host work outside the GPU step: per-request queueing (tokenization and preprocessing) delays enqueue, creating an event gap, but does not occupy the GPU; per-output-token processing adds to TTFT/E2E metrics but does not affect step scheduling. So simulated E2E exceeds a theoretical M/M/k E2E, most at high load. To compare with a theoretical model, use rho_eff = lambda × step_total, not lambda × E2E_total.

docs.title: Per-Request Results
docs.text:
For detailed analysis, save per-request data:

./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-fp8-vllm-tp4.yaml \
  --scenarios <dir of scenario files> --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --rate 100 --num-requests 500 --metrics-path metrics.json

Each request record includes TTFT, E2E, scheduling delay, and completion status.

docs.title: Routing with the llm-d Router
docs.text:
Every cluster simulation routes with the llm-d router, the Endpoint Picker (EPP) of llm-d-router. BLIS has no routing, admission or flow-control logic of its own: it runs the router's real code in-process, configured by the same files a real deployment gives it, and feeds it signals produced by the simulated engines. Two consequences follow.

  • Configuration parity. A deployment's EndpointPickerConfig, its InferencePool, InferenceObjective and InferenceModelRewrite manifests, and its EPP flags run in BLIS unchanged, and the other way around. There is no BLIS-specific routing configuration.
  • Behavioral fidelity. BLIS makes the routing, admission and flow-control decisions the router would make given the same signals. The remaining differences between a simulation and a real deployment come from engine modeling, not from routing.

For instance-level request ordering (the engine's own scheduler), see Scheduling & Priority.

# The router's built-in configuration over four instances (the scenario states no router)
./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml --scenarios testdata/scenarios \
  --registry $PWD/blis-registry --num-instances 4 --rate 100 --num-requests 500

# A real deployment's router configuration, unchanged, named by the scenario's router block
./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node-inferencepool.yaml \
  --scenarios examples/llm-d/scenarios \
  --registry $PWD/blis-registry --num-instances 4 --rate 100 --num-requests 500

docs.title: The router's inputs
docs.text:
The router's inputs are a deployment property, so the scenario states them, as parallel: states the tensor-parallel width: the deployment's router: block and each pool's labels (blis-schemas spec/deployment). There are no router flags for them; --epp-flags, --epp-config, --epp-manifests and --pod-labels were removed, as --tp was, and are refused as unknown flags.

kind: Deployment
name: my-deployment
pools:
  - role: colocated
    nodes: 4
    labels: {app: vllm}          # labels on this pool's model-server pods
    parallel: {tp: 4, pp: 1, dp: 1, enable_expert_parallel: false}
    engine: {...}
router:
  epp_flags: [--pool-name=vllm, --refresh-metrics-interval=20ms]
  endpoint_picker_config: epp-config.yaml   # relative to this scenario file
  manifests: [inferencepool.yaml]
Input Scenario field What it is EPP flags router.epp_flags The router's command-line flags, verbatim, one entry per flag (a Helm chart's epp.flags rendered as --name=value). They select the pool (--pool-name or --endpoint-selector) and set the router's own knobs (--refresh-metrics-interval, --metrics-staleness-threshold, --feature-gates, ...). A --config-file flag is read relative to the scenario file. EndpointPickerConfig router.endpoint_picker_config The router configuration file, as the EPP reads it with --config-file. Naming it here and with an EPP --config-file/--config-text flag is refused. Manifests router.manifests Kubernetes YAML files. The router reads InferencePool, InferenceObjective and InferenceModelRewrite objects through its own reconcilers; other kinds (the model servers' Deployments, Services, ...) are ignored. Pod labels pools[].labels Labels on the pool's simulated model-server pods, so an InferencePool selector or a label filter from a real deployment matches. A label every pool states with one value is on every pod; any other is on its own pool's pods only. BLIS sets llm-d.ai/role from each prefill and decode pool's role (blis-schemas refuses a pool label that contradicts it) and llm-d.ai/inference-serving=true on every pod.

Paths are relative to the scenario file's directory. A file that cannot be read is refused at startup, naming the scenario and the field. Each input is parsed by the router's own code: the flags by the EPP's flag set, the configuration by its config loader, the manifests by its reconcilers. A value the real router rejects is rejected here with the router's message. examples/llm-d/scenarios/ holds scenarios that route with each configuration in examples/llm-d/.

blis run --trace-output records the resolved inputs, inline (the configuration's contents, not its path), in the trace header, with the seed the router ran with, and blis replay routes with them, so a replay reproduces the run's routing whatever --seed it is given (INV-13). A replay whose scenario states no router replays the recorded one. A replay whose scenario does state one (a router block or pool labels) must state the recorded router, and a router environment flag (below) given to replay must match the header's; otherwise the replay is refused, never silently preferred over the header.

Defaults. With no EPP flags, BLIS runs a standalone router whose pool is every simulated pod: --endpoint-selector=llm-d.ai/inference-serving=true --endpoint-target-ports=8000. With no configuration, the router uses its built-in default configuration (queue, KV-cache utilization and prefix-cache scorers). BLIS installs no InferenceObjective of its own: request priorities come only from the deployment's objectives, which the router reconciles for an InferencePool (--pool-name). A request whose objective has no InferenceObjective, and every request in standalone mode, gets priority 0, as in a deployment. examples/llm-d/inferencepool.yaml defines one objective per BLIS SLO class.

As an API server would. The manifests are admitted the way a cluster admits them: custom resources get their CRD defaults (an InferenceObjective poolRef without a group gets inference.networking.k8s.io), both served InferenceObjective versions (llm-d.ai/v1 and llm-d.ai/v1alpha2) are reconciled, unknown or duplicate fields are errors (strict field validation), and a router resource at a version no CRD serves is an error. The CRDs are those of the llm-d-router and Gateway API Inference Extension versions BLIS builds against.

docs.title: The environment around the router
docs.text:
Three BLIS flags model the environment, not routing:

Flag Default Meaning --gateway-latency 0 µs Time from a request's arrival to the router's first look at it: the network and proxy hops before the Endpoint Picker. --epp-scrape-jitter 0 µs Upper bound of a seeded phase offset for each endpoint's metrics collection. At 0 every endpoint is scraped in phase. --kv-event-delay 0 µs Time from an engine publishing its KV-cache events (at the end of a step) to the router's precise-prefix-cache-producer ingesting them: the event transport and the router's processing. At 0 the router has every event of the steps that have ended.

The router itself takes zero simulated time to decide.

EPP flags with no effect. Flags that change how a deployed router is served or observed, never what it decides (--ha-*, --drain-timeout, --tracing, --health-checking, TLS, certificate, gRPC and metrics-endpoint flags, --emit-endpoint-scores), are accepted and have no effect in a simulation; a run that sets one says so on stderr. The legacy metric-name flags (--total-queued-requests-metric, ...) must name a series the simulated engines publish.

Router logs. The router's errors go to stderr as BLIS errors, so they show at every --log level except fatal and panic; its informational messages appear with --log debug or --log trace.

One instance. A single-instance cluster also runs the router: it can only pick that instance, but its admission and flow control still apply. With the default configuration it admits every request at once, and results are identical to a run without a router.

docs.title: What the router sees
docs.text:
Everything the router reads comes from the simulated engines, with real engine semantics.

Inside a DP replica (#1909): a scenario with dp > 1 on an MoE model shows the router one endpoint per replica. The cluster itself then picks the rank with vLLM v0.31.0's own balancer formula, its 100 ms coordinator period and the per-assignment waiting increment (data_parallel_load_balancing internal, the default, or hybrid; under external the router sees every rank). See Latency Models.

  • Requests. Each arrival is the request Envoy would hand the router: an OpenAI /v1/completions body whose prompt is the request's tokens, with max_tokens and stream. The model is the deployment's model, or the request's LoRA adapter. The headers carry x-llm-d-inference-objective (the request's SLO class), x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id (its tenant), when the request has a TTFT target x-llm-d-slo-ttft-ms, and when it has a client timeout x-llm-d-inference-ttl: its lifetime (deadline minus arrival) as a Go duration. Flow control takes the shorter of that and the configured queue budget (60 s by default), and an edf-ordering-policy orders by it; the client still gives up at its deadline, counted as timed out. The router's request handler, parser and Director process it exactly as in a deployment.
  • Multimodal requests. A request carrying image, audio or video tokens is sent as a client sends media: a chat completion (/v1/chat/completions) whose message has an image_url, input_audio or video_url part per modality. The router's token producer sees the media items (its estimate backend from the parts; a vLLM render backend from BLIS's simulated renderer, which renders the request's tokens with each modality's placeholder span, after the text, and a hash of that span). With an encode pool, always-disagg-multimodal-decider then sends such a request to the encode pods the router picks (every one in x-llm-d-encoder-hosts-ports, in order); as in BLIS's own encode stage, encoding takes no simulated time, and the choice is recorded in the decision trace and on the request.
  • Prompt content. BLIS token values are placeholders: a workload models prompt lengths and which prompts share a prefix, nothing more, and a replayed trace draws new placeholder values. The router, which hashes prompt content, is therefore shown canonical tokens: each KV block of a prompt (the last one possibly partial) is identified by its prefix chain, and every chain has fixed canonical tokens. Two prompts are equal exactly where they share a chain of whole blocks, as the engines' prefix caches see them, so a router block size that is a multiple of the engine's block size hashes the canonical prompt as it would the original, and a run and its replay show the router identical prompts.
  • Metrics. Each engine publishes vLLM's Prometheus series at the end of every step, with vLLM's semantics: vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:num_requests_running, vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, vllm:num_preemptions_total, vllm:cache_config_info and, when LoRA is active, vllm:lora_requests_info with the running and waiting adapter sets. The router scrapes them on its own schedule (--refresh-metrics-interval) through its own data source and extractor, so a scrape that lands mid-step sees the previous step's values, as in vLLM. Endpoints present at the start of a run have been scraped before the first request arrives; their periodic scrapes then keep their --epp-scrape-jitter phase. Endpoints that appear later (autoscaling, lifecycle) start cold, as on discovery.
  • KV-cache events. With a precise-prefix-cache-producer in the configuration, each engine publishes vLLM's KV events: a stored block when a block hash enters its prefix cache (a full prefill or decode block, or one reloaded from a CPU tier) and a removed block when one leaves, at the end of the step, as vLLM does. The router receives them --kv-event-delay later, in order per engine, and ingests them synchronously (no ZMQ subscriber). The events carry the blocks' tokens as the router saw them, so the router's index holds, per pod, exactly the blocks the engine can serve from its cache. A terminated instance's blocks are cleared. Speculative indexing (speculativeIndexing) expires its entries on simulated time. With a CPU KV tier (--kv-cpu-blocks, or the --kv-offload-config chain), a block that becomes ready on the CPU tier, or leaves it, is published as a location event on tier cpu, in the same ordered stream, so the router indexes each block on every tier that holds it. A file-system tier behind the CPU tier publishes only when its enable_kv_events is set (vLLM's default is off): a block written to it is a location event on tier shared_storage, the medium llm-d's file-system backend publishes, which the prefix scorer weighs 0.4 by default (kvCacheBackendConfigs). With it off, the router cannot follow a block whose only copy is on that tier: when the block is promoted back to the CPU tier, its location event names a block the router has forgotten and is skipped, as llm-d skips it. A terminated instance's clear travels the same delayed stream, after every batch the instance published. A chain's canonical tokens stay fixed until the router has received the last removal of its block.
  • Prompt rendering. The token-producer plugin's vLLM backend calls a render endpoint; the simulated model server answers it with the request's token IDs.
  • Responses. The router sees the response headers when the engine accepts a streaming request, the first chunk when the first token is delivered, and the final chunk, with usage (prompt tokens and the tokens actually generated), when the response completes. A non-streaming response arrives whole at completion. A request that times out or is dropped ends with the termination cause the router's stream handler would report.
  • Endpoints. Instances are pods of the pool, reconciled by the router's pod reconciler: ready while the instance is routable, not ready while it loads, drains or terminates.

docs.title: Topology identity in kernel-backed scenarios
docs.text:
For a kernel-backed scenario without node_pools, each synthetic Pod gets the host of its engine rank from the same placement used to price P/D KV transfer. If cluster.gpus_per_rack is declared, it gets that rack too. The real router's topology-extractor, topology-affinity-filter and topology-affinity-scorer read those labels through their normal Pod reconciler. Pass --allow-experimental-plugins for these alpha plugins.

A scenario does not say which zone or region contains a node. To model those levels, include one explicit Kubernetes Node document per used simulated host in router.manifests. Its metadata.name must match the simulated host, such as blis-node-0, and it must declare both topology.kubernetes.io/zone and topology.kubernetes.io/region. BLIS matches the worker's actual placement to that Node, copies only those declared levels onto the synthetic Pod, and refuses missing, conflicting or inconsistent rack → zone → region mappings. These Node documents are simulation fixtures, not a live Kubernetes API lookup or a replacement for the router's deployable manifests. Without them, BLIS does not invent zone or region. A zone/region choice can change routing, but the current kernel has no separate cross-zone or cross-region transfer price: those paths retain its inter-node fabric price.

The real topology-stamp-handler can also write the selected prefiller's location to the response's x-peer-topology header. BLIS runs one embedded Endpoint Picker, so it exercises the handler's actual header output but does not forward that header through a coordinator to a second decode picker. Configurations that read peerTopologyHeader remain refused. The signal is fixed when a worker Pod appears, rather than refreshed by an engine-metrics scrape.

This is topology-plugin support for the placements BLIS can represent, within topology issue #1962. A kernel scenario combined with node_pools still has two independent placement systems, so topology plugins are refused until their relation to KV-transfer pricing can be checked. A rank spanning multiple nodes cannot claim one host. A single endpoint grouping multiple data-parallel ranks is also refused for topology routing; without a topology plugin, BLIS adds no derived host label to it. Same-host P/D placement and transfer pricing are a separate follow-up.

BLIS refuses custom topology label keys, coordinator peer-topology headers and missing extractor references. The real router's affinity filter deliberately fails open if its scheduling stage has no peer or no candidate meets the requested affinity. A tighter match can satisfy a looser minAffinity: same-rack endpoints can match minAffinity: zone even without a zone label. That is a router policy rule, not evidence of a local transfer path.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The router's decision becomes a BLIS dispatch:

  • the endpoint it picks serves the request;
  • under disaggregation, the prefill endpoint the disagg-profile-handler names in x-llm-d-prefiller-host-port runs the prefill, and the KV moves to the picked endpoint, which serves the response. KV transfer is priced by the latency kernel, as before;
  • a request the router does not dispatch lands in exactly one INV-1 bucket:
Router outcome BLIS bucket Admission denial: an admitter plugin, or the legacy admission controller shedding a sheddable request (priority < 0) from a saturated pool rejected_requests (admission) No endpoint can serve it (no candidates, every filter or screener eliminated all) routing_rejections Flow control rejects it: queues at capacity gateway_queue_rejected It waits in flow control past its queue-wait budget (TTL) gateway_expired Its client deadline passes while the router holds it (the client disconnects; the router cancels it) timed_out_requests It is still waiting in flow control when the run ends gateway_queue_depth

The outcomes are an explicit allow-list keyed on the router's status code and its x-llm-d-request-dropped-reason. A rejection that matches none of them (an internal error, a malformed request) is not a routing outcome: it ends the run with an error rather than being counted as shedding. So does a run in which the router holds requests that nothing can release.

With --trace-level decisions, each routing record carries the scores the router's primary scheduling profile gave every endpoint; --counterfactual-k ranks them.

docs.title: Fidelity, and BLIS's former router
docs.text:
The acceptance criterion is behavioral fidelity to llm-d: given the same configuration and the same signals, BLIS makes the decisions the router makes. It is not agreement with BLIS's former native router, which ranked instances on instantaneous engine state that no real router has. The two agree where routing cannot matter and differ, as they should, where signal freshness does.

Measured on llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node, seed 42 (BLIS main at 0d092d4e vs this branch, the same kernel and schemas; mean TTFT / p99 TTFT in ms):

Workload Former native router llm-d default configuration llm-d with examples/llm-d/inflight-load.yaml 4 instances, 10 req/s, 800 requests 87.7 / 119.4 87.5 / 118.6 87.7 / 119.4 4 instances, 40 req/s, 2000 requests 96.8 / 129.6 184.6 / 385.1 105.5 / 189.7 8 instances, 80 req/s, 3000 requests 95.5 / 129.5 401.8 / 964.5 105.4 / 186.0

Completed requests agree exactly, and E2E latency and throughput within 1.2%, in every cell. The difference is placement under load:

  • The default configuration ranks endpoints only on scraped metrics. llm-d scrapes at --refresh-metrics-interval (50 ms, which is also the minimum it accepts), and a vLLM engine updates its gauges only at the end of a step, so between scrapes every request sees the same ranking and goes to the same endpoint. That herding is what the real router does with this configuration; it is the effect a capacity plan should see.
  • The router's own in-flight bookkeeping is current at every decision. A configuration that scores on it, as examples/llm-d/inflight-load.yaml does with llm-d's inflight-load-producer and active-request-scorer, comes within 10% of the former router's mean TTFT.
  • --epp-scrape-jitter (here 50 ms) de-phases the endpoints' scrapes and moves the default configuration's mean TTFT by 6-7%; staleness, not phase, dominates.

What is not yet measured: a comparison against traces of a real llm-d deployment.

docs.title: Supported plugins
docs.text:
A configuration may use these plugin types. Each was audited in the router fork (every clock read, background loop, blocking wait and random draw it makes goes through the hosting runtime), and BLIS allows it because every signal it consumes is supplied by simulated engines or explicit cluster state. The fork refuses the types it cannot host; BLIS refuses, through the router's plugin policy, the types whose signals the simulation does not produce.

Kind Types Profile handlers and pickers single-profile-handler, disagg-profile-handler, max-score-picker, random-picker, weighted-random-picker Filters decode-filter, prefill-filter, encode-filter, label-selector-filter, topology-affinity-filter (kernel-backed placement) Scorers queue-scorer, kv-cache-utilization-scorer, prefix-cache-scorer, load-aware-scorer, running-requests-size-scorer, lora-affinity-scorer, token-load-scorer, no-hit-lru-scorer, active-request-scorer, context-length-aware, topology-affinity-scorer (kernel-backed placement) P/D deciders always-disagg-pd-decider, prefix-based-pd-decider Data producers approx-prefix-cache-producer, precise-prefix-cache-producer (fed by the engines' KV events), inflight-load-producer, token-producer (estimate backend, or vLLM backend with a fixed URL) Admission probabilistic-admitter Saturation detectors utilization-detector, concurrency-detector, max-saturation-detector Flow control global-strict-fairness-policy, round-robin-fairness-policy, fcfs-ordering-policy, edf-ordering-policy, slo-deadline-ordering-policy, static-usage-limit-policy, strict-band-selection-policy, priority-holdback-policy, soft-reflective-ceiling-policy Data layer metrics-data-source, core-metrics-extractor, endpoint-notification-source, topology-extractor (kernel-backed placement) Response handlers topology-stamp-handler (emits the header; no coordinator forwarding) Request parsers openai-parser, vllmhttp-parser, sglanghttp-parser, anthropic-parser, passthrough-parser, vertexai-parser

The flow-control layer (featureGates: [flowControl]) runs in full: priority bands, capacity limits, queue-wait budgets, the 1 ms dispatch tick and the 1 s expiry sweep.

docs.title: Refused at startup
docs.text:
Anything that cannot be simulated faithfully is refused before the simulation starts, with the reason. Nothing degrades silently. Plugins are checked after the configuration is loaded and before any of them does work, wherever the configuration references them: under plugins:, or only through a reference such as a flow-control fairnessPolicyRef.

What Why burst-prefix-cache-producer It blocks a request on a sealing timer the hosting runtime does not model. predicted-latency-producer, latency-scorer, latency-slo-admitter, slo-headroom-tier-filter, prefix-cache-affinity-filter They call or consume an external latency-predictor service. latency-observer-producer-hub, latency-observation-scorer-hub, session-state-producer, program-aware-fairness, disaggregatedset-rollout-screener, utilization-filter, request-attribute-reporter Not yet audited for, or not yet moved onto, the hosting runtime. session-affinity-*, session-id-producer, agent-identity, outlen-bucket, header-profile-handler, header-label-affinity-scorer, endpoint-pin-screener The simulated workload does not send the headers they read. mm-embeddings-* The simulated media have no content of their own, so there is no embedding to cache. p2p-source-producer, selective-kv-policy Peer KV pulls are not modeled by the simulated engines. peerTopologyHeader across separate EPPs BLIS runs one EPP and does not model a coordinator forwarding stamped topology to a second EPP; the stamp handler’s response-header output is supported. endpoint-attribute-*, label-producer, dcgm-* The simulated pods carry no custom attributes or GPU telemetry. models-data-source, models-data-extractor, models-responder The simulated engines do not serve /v1/models yet; the workload sends only completions. redis-syncer, thunder-agent, k8s-notification-source, k8s-peer-discovery, file-discovery, multicluster-* They need external services or another discovery source than the simulated deployment. More than one InferencePool; objective or rewrite manifests with --endpoint-selector A run has one router for one pool; in standalone mode the router does not reconcile objectives or rewrites. A pool with more than one target port Several ports make each pod several endpoints (data-parallel ranks behind one pod); BLIS simulates each rank as its own pod. Prefill and decode pools with a configuration that has no disagg-profile-handler The router would serve every request from one flat pool; pass a disaggregating configuration (for example examples/llm-d/pd.yaml). An encode pool on the command line (--encode-instances) No scenario describes the engine an encode pod runs (a blis-schemas deployment's roles are colocated, prefill and decode), as on BLIS main. Encode pools are available through the Go API (DeploymentConfig.EncodeInstances). A token-producer whose vLLM backend discovers endpoints (vllm.endpointDiscovery) It probes pods for model limits on its own schedule, outside the simulation. Use a fixed url, or the estimate backend. A precise-prefix-cache-producer whose tokenProcessorConfig.blockSizeTokens (default 16) is not the engines' KV block size Its keys would never match the engines' blocks. A precise-prefix-cache-producer with a Redis or cost-aware index, or non-vLLM kvEventsConfig.engineType; with LoRA adapters in the deployment Redis is an external service; the cost-aware index's lookups have no fixed order; the engines publish vLLM's events and their prefix caches do not key blocks by adapter. A core-metrics-extractor that, for some pod, reads an engine other than vLLM (by defaultEngine or the pod's engine label, llm-d.ai/engine-type by default), or a vLLM mapping naming series the engines do not publish; a metrics-data-source path other than /metrics The simulated engines publish vLLM's series at /metrics; anything else would read nothing.

Also outside the model: conditional decode (Prefer: if-available), and the P/D sidecar's MoRIIO parallel prefill-and-decode dispatch (BLIS always runs prefill, then the KV transfer, then decode). BLIS hosts the router's Endpoint Picker only: llm-d's coordinator and its E/P/D pipeline: (multimodal encode, then prefill, then decode, as in llm-d's coordinator disaggregation guide) are not simulated, so E/P/D parity is the EPP's decisions alone.

docs.title: From BLIS's former routing features
docs.text:
BLIS no longer has its own routing, admission or flow control. Each former feature either maps to an llm-d configuration or is dropped.

Former BLIS feature llm-d configuration --routing-policy weighted --routing-scorers ... A scheduling profile with the matching scorers and weights, and max-score-picker. scorer prefix-affinity approx-prefix-cache-producer + prefix-cache-scorer scorer precise-prefix-cache precise-prefix-cache-producer + prefix-cache-scorer (with a token-producer), indexing the engines' KV events scorers queue-depth, kv-utilization, active-requests, running-requests, load-aware, no-hit-lru queue-scorer, kv-cache-utilization-scorer, active-request-scorer, running-requests-size-scorer, load-aware-scorer, no-hit-lru-scorer --lora-scorer-weight lora-affinity-scorer in the profile --routing-policy round-robin, least-loaded, always-busiest; scorers load-balance, vllm-dp Dropped: the llm-d router has no such policy. The nearest configurations are random-picker, and queue-scorer or load-aware-scorer with max-score-picker. --admission-policy gaie-legacy The router's default admission: with the flowControl gate off, the legacy admission controller sheds sheddable requests (priority < 0) when the saturation detector reports a saturated pool. Its thresholds are utilization-detector parameters. --admission-policy tier-shed InferenceObjective priorities with the legacy admission controller, or flow-control priority bands and a usage-limit policy. --admission-policy token-bucket, reject-all; tenant_budgets Dropped. Per-tenant fairness is the fairness ID (the request's tenant) with round-robin-fairness-policy. --flow-control featureGates: [flowControl] --saturation-detector, --queue-depth-threshold, --kv-cache-util-threshold, --max-concurrency utilization-detector or concurrency-detector and their parameters --dispatch-order fifo, slo-deadline; --slo-targets fcfs-ordering-policy, slo-deadline-ordering-policy --fairness-policy global-strict-fairness-policy, round-robin-fairness-policy --max-gateway-queue-depth, --per-band-capacity flowControl.maxRequests, a priority band's capacity --usage-limit-threshold static-usage-limit-policy --request-ttl flowControl.defaultRequestTTL --queue-shedding, --dispatch-tick-interval, --in-flight-eviction Dropped: BLIS-only behaviors. llm-d's dispatch tick is fixed at 1 ms; its in-flight eviction is flowControl.enableEviction (admission). --pd-decider always, prefix-threshold; --pd-prefix-threshold disagg-profile-handler with always-disagg-pd-decider or prefix-based-pd-decider (nonCachedTokens) --prefill-routing-scorers, --decode-routing-scorers The prefill and decode scheduling profiles --encode-decider The disaggregation handler's encode decider (always-disagg-multimodal-decider for multimodal) --admission-latency, --routing-latency --gateway-latency --snapshot-refresh-interval The EPP flag --refresh-metrics-interval: staleness now comes from the scrape itself --cache-signal-delay --kv-event-delay: a fixed delay from an engine publishing its KV events to the router ingesting them (the old flag refreshed a snapshot of every cache at most every 50 ms) examples/epp-*.yaml The llm-d configurations themselves (deploy/config/ in llm-d-router)

docs.text:

  • Architecture — how the router is embedded.
  • The llm-d router fork — how the fork hosts the router and how it is kept current.
  • Invariants — INV-1, INV-6, INV-7, INV-9 and INV-13 as they apply to the router.

docs.title: Scheduling & Priority
docs.text:
Routing decides which instance receives a request. Scheduling decides what order requests are processed within an instance. These are independent policy axes — you can combine any router configuration with any scheduler.

# Priority-FCFS scheduling with SLO-class-based priority in a 4-instance cluster
./blis run --scenario llama-3.1-70b-instruct-h200-tp4-4node.yaml --scenarios testdata/scenarios \
  --registry $PWD/blis-registry \
  --num-instances 4 --rate 100 --num-requests 500 \
  --scheduler priority-fcfs
# SLO class is set in the workload spec (slo_class: critical/standard/batch/etc.)

docs.title: How Priority Works
docs.text:
Request priority is static — set once when the request enters the instance, and never changed.

At enqueue time (EnqueueRequest and EnqueueDecodeSubRequest), the simulator converts the request's SLOClass to a vLLM-convention priority value via SLOPriorityMap.InvertForVLLM(SLOClass):

critical   → Priority 0.0  (most urgent)
standard   → Priority 1.0
batch      → Priority 5.0
sheddable  → Priority 6.0
background → Priority 7.0  (least urgent)

This follows vLLM's convention: lower integer = more urgent. The llm-d router (admission, flow control, routing) uses the llm-d convention (higher = more urgent), with priorities from its InferenceObjectives (see Admission Control); the inversion happens at the cluster→instance dispatch boundary.

SLO class is set in your workload spec:

clients:
  - slo_class: critical
    rate: 10
  - slo_class: standard
    rate: 50

Custom priority values can be overridden via the policy bundle:

priority:
  slo_priorities:
    batch: 0   # make batch non-sheddable

docs.title: Available Schedulers
docs.text:
Each scheduler implements the InstanceScheduler interface: a single OrderQueue method called every step to reorder the wait queue before batch formation.

Scheduler Flag Value Strategy Notes FCFS --scheduler fcfs First-Come-First-Served. No reordering — requests are processed in arrival order. Default. Fair and predictable. Priority-FCFS --scheduler priority-fcfs Sort by priority ascending (lower value = more urgent, vLLM convention), then by arrival time ascending within the same priority. Ties broken by request ID for determinism. Useful when SLOClass is set in the workload spec. Without SLO classes, all requests get Priority=1.0 (standard) and this degrades to FCFS by arrival tiebreak. SJF --scheduler sjf Shortest Job First. Sort by input token count ascending, then by arrival time, then by ID. Optimizes TTFT for short requests but can starve long ones under sustained load. Ignores Request.Priority entirely. Reverse-priority --scheduler reverse-priority Sort by priority descending (highest value = least urgent scheduled first). Pathological template for testing only — deliberately causes priority inversions.

All schedulers use sort.SliceStable for deterministic ordering (INV-6).

docs.title: How Scheduling and Priority Interact
docs.text:
The scheduler and priority are composed at each simulation step:

  1. Priority is already set (static — set at enqueue via SLOPriorityMap.InvertForVLLM, not recomputed per step).
  2. Queue reordering: Call InstanceScheduler.OrderQueue() on the wait queue.
  3. Batch formation: Dequeue requests from the front of the reordered queue into the running batch.

Common combinations:

Combination Effective Behavior priority-fcfs + mixed SLO classes Critical requests scheduled first, background last. priority-fcfs + uniform SLO class All priorities equal — degrades to FCFS by arrival time. sjf + any SLO class SJF by input length (priority ignored). fcfs + any SLO class FCFS by arrival time (priority computed but reordering skipped).

docs.title: Preemption and Re-enqueueing
docs.text:
BLIS models vLLM's two-queue architecture (WaitQ + RunningBatch). When a request is preempted from the running batch due to KV cache pressure:

  • The request is placed at the front of the WaitQ (not the back).
  • Its progress is reset to zero (recompute mode, matching vLLM's recompute preemption).
  • On the next step, the scheduler reorders the full queue including the preempted request.

This means preempted requests get implicit priority over fresh arrivals in FCFS mode. With priority-fcfs and mixed SLO classes, the preempted request's static priority determines its position relative to other waiting requests.

By default (--preemption-policy fcfs), the tail of the running batch is evicted. When --preemption-policy priority is set, the least-urgent running request is evicted — the one with the highest Priority value (vLLM convention: background=7 is least urgent and evicted first). Among equal-priority requests, the most recently arrived is evicted first. This matches vLLM's --scheduling-policy priority preemption behavior (vLLM v0.31.0 vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:765,777). A scenario stating engine.scheduling_policy: priority selects both priority-fcfs queueing and priority preemption, as vLLM does (fcfs selects fcfs for both); in a prefill/decode deployment each pool takes its own engine's policy. An explicit flag overrides the scenario and is recorded in the results file (Scenario Overrides).

docs.title: When to Use Which
docs.text:
Workload Recommended Configuration Why Uniform traffic, no SLO differentiation --scheduler fcfs (default) No reordering needed. All requests are equivalent. Mixed SLO classes (critical vs background) --scheduler priority-fcfs with slo_class in workload spec Critical requests get Priority=0, scheduled before background (Priority=7). Latency-sensitive short requests --scheduler sjf Short prompts get processed first. Watch for starvation of long requests under sustained load. Low load (< ~10 req/s) Any Batch sizes are small enough that all schedulers pick the same requests. At low load, all schedulers produce equivalent results within ~5%.

SJF starvation risk

Under sustained high load, SJF can indefinitely delay long-prompt requests as short ones keep arriving. BLIS does not currently implement aging or starvation guards for SJF. If your workload has a mix of short and long prompts at high utilization, prefer --scheduler priority-fcfs with SLO classes instead.
